articles.title_orig: US reinvents rare earth refining as China guards know-how
articles.title_zh: US reinvents rare earth refining as China guards know-how
articles.content_orig:
Keep independent journalism alive
With Beijing keeping its rare earth refining technology, equipment and technicians at home, Washington is funding private refiners to develop new ways to process the strategic metals rather than copying Chinese methods.
A senior US official told Asia Times that American refiners would rely on their own innovation to make the country self-sufficient in critical minerals, and that she was confident they would succeed.
Industry experts, however, said some US projects would still have to pay high costs to learn China’s traditional extraction method, which Chinese firms have spent more than two decades perfecting.
“Over the last 20 years, we’ve developed a lot of innovation, but we didn’t develop the manufacturing know-how,” Audrey Robertson, assistant secretary of energy at the Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation of the US Department of Energy (DOE), told Asia Times at the Financial Times Metals & Mining Summit in London on October 15.
“We might develop the intellectual property, but we don’t execute on building the big factory. There’s definitely going to be an increased focus on getting innovation that starts and stays in the United States, and the ability to build out the critical mineral processing with new and innovative methods,” she said.
She said the US would not close the supply chain gap by doing what it had been doing for the past 20 years, but by finding new solutions and new ways of doing things.
Washington’s push comes as Beijing has steadily tightened its grip on rare earths, restricting exports of the metals as well as the technology and people needed to refine them.
In December 2023, Beijing banned exports of rare earth processing and magnet-making technologies. In June, it cut off supplies of China-origin dual-use items to US producers MP Materials and USA Rare Earth. Last month, it tightened exit rules to stop skilled technicians, including rare earth experts, from leaving the country.
Since last year, the Trump administration has taken a series of measures to boost the country’s capability in rare earth refining:
Robertson said the US faces a workforce shortage in the critical mineral sector and that the PROSPECT initiative aims to double the number of mining and minerals graduates within two years.
“The US has a history of having problems and then finding solutions. Twenty years ago, we were the world’s largest importer of oil and natural gas. Now we are the largest exporter of both,” she said. “We changed that not by competing with OPEC but by innovating in the US. We are going to attack critical minerals and processing with the same drive to solve the problem.”
Robertson did not say what new methods the US will use, but company disclosures point to continuous ion chromatography (CIC) and electrochemical separation.
In China, refiners dissolve the minerals in strong acid, mix the solution with kerosene and chemicals such as P507 and P204, and pass it through hundreds of mixing and settling tanks. A stronger acid then strips out each element so it can be precipitated.
US firms using CIC also dissolve minerals in acid, then dilute the solution with water and run it through resin-filled columns, where each element moves at its own speed and emerges separately. The US dropped chromatography in the 1950s due to cost concerns. With rare earths now dubbed the new gold, the cost is worth it.
In electrochemical separation, rare earths are dissolved in molten salt at about 700°C and an electric current is applied. As each element turns into metal at a slightly different voltage, they can be collected separately.
“I think the innovation will be divided. There are certain mainstream technologies that are relatively widely available, but in the rare earth and magnet value chain, this is a piece of process capability that the West has transferred to China and doesn’t have anymore,” said Michel Van Hoey, a senior partner at McKinsey, at the same panel.
He said China has continued to advance that capability over the past 40 years, and the West will have to catch up to close the gap if it wants to be independent of China.
US refiners are taking different approaches.
On Tuesday, Phoenix Tailings said it will build Freedom Separation, a US$375 million rare earth separation facility in Rochester, New York, to process more than 18,000 tons of feedstock into over 4,400 tons of separated rare earth oxides a year by 2028. In June, the company secured a US$500 million conditional loan from the Pentagon and a US$66 million DOE grant.
Japan has felt the squeeze most. After Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said last November that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could pose an existential threat to Japan, Beijing on January 6 banned exports of dual-use items, including some rare earths, to Japanese military users.
The Financial Times reported on Tuesday that Japan could run out of yttrium within months and had asked Washington to help press Beijing to ease its curbs.
Yttrium, a heat-resistant metal, coats jet engines and chipmaking equipment, and US defense supply chains rely on Japanese components that contain it. Yttrium oxide prices outside China have jumped 179-fold in two years to US$1,150 per kilogram, against US$9 in China, according to Argus. “It is true that exports of yttrium have stalled not only to Japan but worldwide, causing a supply-demand crunch and soaring prices,” an official at Japan’s industry ministry told the media on Wednesday. On October 13, Toronto-listed Aclara Resources said its planned heavy rare earth separation facility at the Port of Vinton in Louisiana would cost about US$494 million. In the second half of 2028, it is expected to produce about 1,350 tons of yttrium oxide a year, along with neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr), dysprosium, terbium, gadolinium and samarium oxides.
Aclara will use large-scale solvent extraction to separate mixed rare earth carbonate shipped from its projects in Brazil and Chile. It’s unclear whether the company will source P507 and P204 extractants from China or buy more expensive substitutes in the US and Germany.
Asked by Asia Times whether Washington’s critical mineral strategy would work, Laura Konkel, senior counsel at law firm Akin Gump, said not every project in the US will succeed, but the sheer number of deals and an unprecedented scale of government capital make success more likely, with the onus now on the industry to deliver on timelines and milestones.

articles.title_zh: Powerful earthquake in China’s Tibet collapses hundreds of homes and kills at least 16 people
articles.content_orig:
A magnitude 7 earthquake hit China’s southwestern region of Tibet at about 10:33pm (14:33 GMT) on Thursday, killing 16 people and injuring 32 others, state ‌news agency Xinhua reported, citing Nagqu City’s emergency management bureau.
Eleven of the injured were in serious condition, while 21 sustained minor injuries, Xinhua added.
A level-II earthquake disaster emergency response was activated in the area, the news agency said.
The US Geological Survey said that the earthquake’s epicentre was in a mountainous area about 190km east-northeast of Nagqu and 390km northeast of the regional capital Lhasa.
Local authorities have found at least two people injured in a village near the epicentre, with some houses in villages closest to the epicentre showing cracks, according to Xinhua.
Videos released by local state media showed people leaving their ⁠homes and seeking shelter outside or in ⁠their cars parked on the street.
The earthquake is ‌the strongest to hit China since January 2024.

articles.title_orig: Moderna, Merck shares fall on eagerly anticipated cancer vaccine results
articles.title_zh: Moderna, Merck shares fall on eagerly anticipated cancer vaccine results
articles.content_orig:
Moderna shares dropped as much as 25% on Thursday following the leak of partial data on its closely watched cancer vaccine developed with Merck .
Shares of both drugmakers fell even though the data, released in full later Thursday following the leak, appeared meaningful for patients and positive relative to Wall Street expectations.
The personalized vaccine, known as intismeran autogene, paired with Merck's immunotherapy Keytruda reduced the risk of recurrence or death in certain melanoma patients by 42% compared with Keytruda alone.
The data also showed that the shot along with Keytruda reduced the risk of cancer spreading to distant parts of the body or death by 38%, compared with just the immunotherapy.
The companies said about 82% of patients who received the personalized cancer vaccine alongside Keytruda were alive without their melanoma returning at two years after receiving the shot, compared with 70% of those who received Keytruda alone.
"This is a huge development for our patients," said Dr. Hussein Tawbi, a melanoma expert and trial investigator at the University of Texas MD ​Anderson Cancer Center, about the results.
He said that the added benefit of the vaccine also comes with much milder toxicity, or side effects like injection-site pain, compared to other cancer treatments.
The detailed phase 3 trial results were set to be presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology conference this weekend.
"Whenever you put a therapy on top of something that works really well, like Keytruda, sometimes it's harder to show additional benefit. We have no problems of showing additional benefit here," Dr. Dean Li, Merck Research Laboratories president, said in an interview ahead of the results.
The benefit appeared even larger after the six-month vaccine regimen, with a separate analysis showing a 58% reduction in risk of recurrence or death. The companies say it is still too early to determine whether the treatment helps patients live longer overall.
Several analysts acknowledged investors' elevated expectations ahead of the release, but noted that the data is overall positive.
"We assert this relative reduction in recurrence/death is clinically meaningful," BMO Capital Markets analyst Evan Seigerman said in a research note on Thursday following the leak. "Such a [stock] reaction likely reflects inflated expectations into the full data release, rather than a true indictment on the efficacy of the combo therapy."
Oncologists and investors see the targeted vaccine as a possible breakthrough treatment, with the potential to be used to treat other forms of cancer in the future. Merck and Moderna are studying the vaccine in several trials across other tumors, such as non-small cell lung cancer, bladder cancer and renal cell carcinoma.
But Li acknowledged the companies have more work to show the product can be effective across tumor types.
"I can dream of creating a log cabin, but we got some wood chops, and we've just knocked down one tree," Li said. "Knocking one tree does not give you a cabin or a village."
The shot is designed to target the specific mutations in each patient's tumor rather than using a one-size-fits-all approach. The idea is to train the immune system to recognize and kill those unique cancer markers and then pair that response with Keytruda, which helps the body attack the cancer more effectively.
It could also offer Moderna a critical additional commercial product in its pipeline, following vaccines for Covid-19, the flu and respiratory syncytial virus.
In a research note Thursday, UBS analysts said "this is overall a strong data set" and gives more confidence in upcoming studies of the vaccine in kidney and bladder cancers. They added the stock reaction may be due more to massive expectations than disappointing data.
Against the backdrop of those high expectations, Moderna shares have spiked more than 530% year-to-date as of Thursday afternoon.
Shares of Merck, a much larger drugmaker, fell by about 1% on Thursday. The company's stock has climbed nearly 41% this year.
Since the vaccine is personalized, the complicated manufacturing process can take six weeks. But Merck CEO Robert Davis told CNBC last week that the company believes it can shorten that timeline in the future, potentially allowing the shot to reach more patients more quickly.

articles.title_orig: Zuckerberg makes deal with Meta to help him pay billionaire tax if it passes
articles.title_zh: Zuckerberg makes deal with Meta to help him pay billionaire tax if it passes
articles.content_orig:
Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg
Meta has agreed to a new deal with chief executive Mark Zuckerberg to prevent him from leaving California over a proposed state tax on billionaires.
The agreement gives Zuckerberg, whose wealth is estimated to exceed $200bn (Â£149bn), even more shares in Meta to make up for the fraction of his fortune he may lose if the tax wins voter approval in November.
The measure would impose a one-time 5% tax on residents with a net worth of more than $1bn. It would likely see the Facebook co-founder pay around $10bn in additional state taxes.
He secured the deal with a special committee of Meta after "robust" and "at several points, contentious" negotiations, according to a Wednesday financial disclosure.
California is home to most of the US's technology giants and there are around 225 billionaires who reside in the state, according to the Americans for Tax Fairness campaign group.
The wealth of such people, including Zuckerberg, has ballooned in recent years. Meanwhile, his estimated effective tax rate in California was less than 1% , external each year.
Nevertheless, Zuckerberg told Meta's board last month that he was thinking of moving his primary residence out of California, and even selling his property in the state. His main homes in Californa are in Palo Alto and Lake Tahoe.
Such a move "would be public and inevitably noted and commented upon by company employees", Zuckerberg told the board.
It would also "raise questions for management of the company going forward", he claimed.
In response, Meta decided to create more shares of stock in the company in order to give Zuckerberg a way to essentially make up any wealth he may lose through the tax proposal.
Through what's known as a stock split announced by the company on Wednesday , Meta created an entirely new type of stock and gave one new share to each existing shareholder. Zuckerberg is one of the company's largest shareholders and famously controls the company through the design of his holdings.
Through the deal, he will receive more stock, more often, and also be able to sell it on a quarterly basis, according to the company's financial filing. The shares will not change his level control over Meta, but they will allow him to cash in more easily on the company's value.
The deal appears to be effective even if the one-time tax in California does not pass, and will go on for eight years - as long as Zuckerberg remains a resident of California.
Meta called the deal with Zuckerberg its "Founder Alignment Agreement," saying it was "critically important" to keep him leading the company from California given the "dramatic and unprecedented transformation taking place in the tech industry and global economy related to artificial intelligence."
The company alluded to problems the company experienced during the Covid-19 pandemic, when Zuckerberg began working outside of the office and mostly from his large compound in Kauai, Hawaii.
After a surge in hiring at Meta during the pandemic, a whistleblower scandal that led to renewed focus on child safety, and a refocus within the company to building out the "metaverse," which included renaming the company Meta from Facebook, the company began mass layoffs and restructuring.
Layoffs have continued into this year. The company's headcount is down 15% from a year ago, meaning it has shed at least 10,000 workers.
Today, the company has moved away from the "metaverse," or virtual platforms, and is more focused on artificial intelligence products and related tools.
With Zuckerberg leading the company's efforts to catch up in the AI race, Meta's board said it sees a future of "tremendous market opportunity" for the company.
Major tech companies are set to spend an estimated $1 trillion , external this year alone developing AI and the costly infrastructure around it, like data centres .
Meta said on Wednesday it planned to spend as much as $145bn this year on AI projects. The company has increased the amount it expects to spend on AI each financial quarter so far this year.
It is spending so much on the technology that it posted negative cash flow for the first time since the company went public 14 years ago. Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments, meaning Meta is now spending more money than it is bringing in.
And the company intends to spend even more in the year ahead. Susan Li, Meta's chief financial officer, said on Wednesday that another benefit of the stock split would be to give the company more ways to finance future spending on AI work.
The degree of the company's spending on AI, without an clear new revenue stream coming from it, appeared to spook investors on Thursday.
Meta's shares fell more than 7%, wiping more than $100bn off of the company's market capitalisation, a key metric used worldwide to measure the value of a publicly-traded company.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX in Talks to Access 80,000 Cell Sites for Wireless Network
articles.title_zh: SpaceX in Talks to Access 80,000 Cell Sites for Wireless Network
articles.content_orig:
On the Oct. 19, 2026, episode of The Morning Filter podcast, host Dave Sekera sat down with director of communication-services equity research Michael Hodel to answer viewer questions about SpaceX’s SPCX purchase of wireless spectrum infrastructure. Here is an excerpt from the show.
David Sekera: Mike, thank you very much for joining us. As you can imagine, we’ve gotten a lot of questions on The Morning Filter regarding what SpaceX is doing following the reports that they started buying some wireless spectrum. The first question I have for you is what do you think they’re doing in the wireless space, and how does that then relate to their satellite network and some of the coverage they’re already able to provide there?
Michael Hodel: I think it’s important first to distinguish what Starlink is doing on the broadband side versus the wireless side. On the broadband side, that’s where the company’s probably gotten the most attention. It’s where you’re putting a dish on a house or on a portable RV, and you’re getting broadband service from the satellite.
What we’re talking about here is something a little bit different. This is direct to the cell, direct to your cellphone, your smartphone, your iPhone, what have you, service from a satellite. What this service has been marketed as traditionally is infill for places where terrestrial networks don’t reach, so a national park or somewhere in the wilderness. There’s been a lot of talk that SpaceX wants to offer a more comprehensive wireless service, and to do that, they need network coverage in more densely populated areas. A satellite service doesn’t have the capacity to serve lots of people in a small space, and it also doesn’t have the ability to penetrate walls.
If you’re indoors, that signal from a satellite’s going to have a hard time getting to you. What this latest move is intended to do is to provide Starlink with the spectrum that it would need to build a network to get that in-building coverage in particular. And this isn’t likely to be spectrum that’s used from satellites. It’s more likely, and SpaceX has said as much, that they’ll build an actual network with towers and rooftops and that sort of thing to use this spectrum, again, to provide that coverage layer that can reach consumers in buildings or in rural areas.
Why that’s interesting is we think Starlink has most likely been trying to negotiate a wholesale agreement with one of the wireless carriers, AT&T T , T-Mobile TMUS , or Verizon VZ , because that would be a much more efficient way for Starlink to fill in where its satellites can’t reach. The prospects of building a wireless network from scratch are extremely daunting. You’re talking billions of dollars for more spectrum, more than what SpaceX has already purchased, billions, tens of billions of dollars to actually build the network, and then billions upon billions of dollars to acquire customers, provide them with phone financing, and the sorts of things that customers expect today. We think right now SpaceX is most likely trying to build up assets to make itself a credible entrant into the wireless market as a way of negotiating aggressively with one of the existing wireless carriers for capacity in those areas where its satellite can’t reach.
Sekera: Do you think this is actually just more a negotiation ploy than it is necessarily them really looking at going head-to-head against the incumbent wireless providers and build out their own complete network?
Hodel: It could be a little bit of both. I think for Starlink and SpaceX, they need to have some sort of fallback plan if they can’t get an agreement with one of the major wireless carriers. And the reason why that’s important is that all three of the major US carriers, again, AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile, have formed a joint venture for dealing with satellite providers where they’ve basically said, “We’re not going to negotiate independently and provide network access to somebody like Starlink who can then just turn around and compete with us.” By collaborating in that way, they’ve ensured that one of the companies, one of the carriers, doesn’t break off and sign an agreement with Starlink and leave the other two behind. And so, SpaceX and Starlink need to have some kind of credible fallback plan to enhance their negotiating position and also to potentially go it alone if the telecom companies don’t ultimately come to the table and agree to some sort of wholesale arrangement for Starlink.
Sekera: Thinking about where AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile are trading today, and based on your view that this is most likely going to be them collaborating with Starlink as opposed to competing directly head-to-head, any of those stocks look interesting to you today? And if so, why?
Hodel: So, the big thing we did in light of Starlink’s latest spectrum purchase, and it does make the company much more credible as a fourth entrant into the wireless market, is we increased our
When I look at the three carriers today, T-Mobile actually looks the most interesting to me. It’s trading at about a 35% discount to our fair value estimate, which is a wider discount than AT&T or Verizon. The stock’s actually offering a decent yield for the first time in its history, above 3%, and they have the financial capacity to buy back stock pretty aggressively as well. And I like T-Mobile’s position in the fixed-line business a little bit more than most people might expect. I think some of the investments that AT&T and Verizon are making to expand their fiber networks actually will struggle to generate attractive returns on capital. But again, I don’t think T-Mobile is quite yet at a large enough margin of safety to really pound the table on it, but it’s the one that I think looks the most attractive here.

articles.title_orig: China-made cancer drug to go on sale in US after Americans travel to buy it
articles.title_zh: China-made cancer drug to go on sale in US after Americans travel to buy it
articles.content_orig:
AstraZeneca moves to make the lung cancer treatment available in the US after lengthy delays raised concerns over patient access
Global pharmaceutical firm AstraZeneca said on Thursday it would start selling a cancer drug after coming under criticism for failing to bring it to the US market faster, prompting some Americans to fly to Shanghai to procure the potentially life-saving medicine first developed by China.
In recent months, desperate Americans have travelled to China to obtain the Chinese-made cancer drug that was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration but remained unavailable in the country for more than a year, according to a cancer-treatment awareness advocate who made the journey while his mother was battling the disease.
Developed by China’s Dizal Pharmaceutical, sunvozertinib is a targeted lung cancer drug designed to treat adults with an advanced form of the illness, offering another treatment option for patients.
“The drug was approved in China in 2023. The FDA approved it in July 2025,” Max Doppelt, chief executive of Patient Data Vault, a consultancy that connects cancer patients to clinical trials, wrote on social media on Wednesday.

articles.title_orig: Russian oil giant Rosneft fears just a few more months of war in Ukraine could inflict lasting damage on its business, Bloomberg reports
articles.title_zh: Russian oil giant Rosneft fears just a few more months of war in Ukraine could inflict lasting damage on its business, Bloomberg reports
articles.content_orig:
Rosneft officials are concerned that even a few more months of the war in Ukraine could cause lasting damage to the company’s business, Bloomberg reported, citing sources.
The company’s finances are deteriorating as profits fall and debt rises, Bloomberg’s sources said, despite expectations that the war in the Middle East would boost its earnings.
Rosneft has suffered significant damage from Ukrainian strikes on its oil refineries. The company operates 12 refineries that account for about a third of Russia’s total refining capacity. According to Bloomberg’s tally, five of the 15 confirmed drone strikes on Russian refineries in September alone targeted Rosneft facilities that supply fuel to European Russia.
The Ryazan refinery, which has repeatedly come under attack, is among the hardest hit. The Syzran refinery has spent most of the past six months either shut down completely or operating at less than a third of capacity. The Tuapse refinery has been shut down since April.
Bloomberg reported that Rosneft managed to restart some refineries within weeks of an attack, only for them to be struck again once repairs were complete or nearly complete. The constant need for repairs is driving costs to levels that cannot be sustained in the long run, the outlet’s sources said. As a result, they said, some plants have deliberately slowed repairs, stretching work that would normally take a few days into weeks.

articles.title_orig: Airbnb guests no longer have to wash the dishes or strip the beds at checkout
articles.title_zh: Airbnb guests no longer have to wash the dishes or strip the beds at checkout
articles.content_orig:
Airbnb has changed its rules to limit what property hosts may ask guests to do - including when it comes to cleaning.
The updated guidelines state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules and can also add other "reasonable" requests.
Airbnb states that guests - who are required to pay a cleaning fee - should not be asked to complete tasks normally done by a cleaner, including washing dishes and stripping beds.
The new rules will apply to all reservations booked on or after 20 November on the accommodation marketplace.
"House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we've heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage," Airbnb told the BBC.
"So, we've redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises."
According to the new requirements on the Airbnb website, hosts are generally not allowed to ask guests to complete tasks that "require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner, including stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes".
The company said it may grant exceptions in some circumstances. For example, guests can be asked to limit shower time if there are local drought-related water restrictions.
A property's rules will be displayed to guests more prominently moving forward and  will appear in the guests' reservation reminders.
Contracts will only be allowed in limited circumstances, including when required by law or homeowners association rules.
While a host will not be able to impose fines, they remain in control of their house rules and requests, the company said.
If a host's request does not follow Airbnb policies, the issue will be flagged and the owner can appeal if they disagree.
Guests have for years complained about unreasonable tasks they we required to complete before departure, especially as they are required to pay cleaning fees.
TikTok videos from Airbnb hosts Cassie and Jon that show them closely inspecting their rental property in the US state of Georgia after guests leave have gone viral recently for their attention to detail.
One video from the couple, for example, accuses guests of "disrespecting the house rules" for leaving a television remote out of place.
They have been criticised for their strict rules and high standards but said in response that their content had been misinterpreted
Their videos have inspired other content creators to parody stringent hosts.

Electricity generation and hydrogen production company Bloom Energy (NYSE:BE) reported Q3 2026 results beating Wall Street's revenue expectations , with sales up 138% year on year to $1.24 billion. The company's full-year revenue guidance of $4.5 billion at the midpoint came in 9.1% above analysts' estimates. Its non-GAAP profit of $0.94 per share was 39.8% above analysts' consensus estimates.

KR Sridhar, Founder, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Bloom Energy, said, "Electricity is the foundation of economic growth, human well-being and national competitiveness. Today, the world is moving from a century-old model of centralized power to a new architecture that includes firm, distributed onsite generation. Bloom is leading that transformation. What began with hyperscalers is rapidly moving across market segments because every business needs reliable power to grow. We are building the electricity platform for the digital era: power where it is needed, when it is needed, clean and always on."
Working in stealth mode for eight years, Bloom Energy (NYSE:BE) designs, manufactures, and markets solid oxide fuel cell systems for on-site power generation.
A company's long-term performance is an indicator of its overall quality. Any business can put up a good quarter or two, but many enduring ones grow for years. Over the last five years, Bloom Energy grew its sales at an incredible 34.2% compounded annual growth rate. Its growth surpassed the average industrials company and shows its offerings resonate with customers, a great starting point for our analysis.
Long-term growth is the most important, but within industrials, a half-decade historical view may miss new industry trends or demand cycles. Bloom Energy's annualized revenue growth of 74.5% over the last two years is above its five-year trend, suggesting its demand was strong and recently accelerated.
Bloom Energy also breaks out the revenue for its most important segment, Product. Over the last two years, Bloom Energy's Product revenue (energy servers and electrolyzers) averaged 110% year-on-year growth. This segment has outperformed its total sales during the same period, lifting the company's performance.
This quarter, Bloom Energy reported magnificent year-on-year revenue growth of 138%, and its $1.24 billion of revenue beat Wall Street's estimates by 14.6%.
Looking ahead, sell-side analysts expect revenue to grow 59.1% over the next 12 months, a deceleration versus the last two years. Despite the slowdown, this projection is healthy and implies the market sees success for its products and services.

Bloom Energy was roughly breakeven when averaging the last five years of quarterly operating profits, inadequate for an industrials business. This result isn't too surprising given its low gross margin as a starting point.
On the plus side, Bloom Energy's operating margin rose by 36.5 percentage points over the last five years, as its sales growth gave it immense operating leverage.
This quarter, Bloom Energy generated an operating margin profit margin of 18.2%, up 16.7 percentage points year on year. The increase was solid, and because its operating margin rose more than its gross margin, we can infer it was more efficient with expenses such as marketing, R&D, and administrative overhead.
We track the long-term change in earnings per share (EPS) for the same reason as long-term revenue growth. Compared to revenue, however, EPS highlights whether a company's growth is profitable.
Bloom Energy's full-year EPS flipped from negative to positive over the last five years. This is a good sign and shows it's at an inflection point.
Like with revenue, we analyze EPS over a more recent period because it can provide insight into an emerging theme or development for the business.
For Bloom Energy, its two-year annual EPS growth of 317% was higher than its five-year trend. We love it when earnings growth accelerates, especially when it accelerates off an already high base.
In Q3, Bloom Energy reported adjusted EPS of $0.94, up from $0.15 in the same quarter last year. This print easily cleared analysts' estimates, and shareholders should be content with the results. Over the next 12 months, Wall Street expects Bloom Energy's full-year EPS to grow 61.5% from $2.61 to $4.22.
It was good to see Bloom Energy beat analysts' EPS expectations this quarter. We were also excited its EBITDA outperformed Wall Street's estimates by a wide margin. Zooming out, we think this was a good print with some key areas of upside. The market seemed to be hoping for more, and the stock traded down 2.6% to $213.14 immediately after reporting.

articles.title_orig: S&P 500, Nasdaq end sharply lower as revived AI doubts ignite tech selloff
articles.title_zh: S&P 500, Nasdaq end sharply lower as revived AI doubts ignite tech selloff
articles.content_orig:
Datacenter and chip costs fueled sharp decrease in AI sector although non-AI stocks still had a strong showing
The latest shudder for stocks in the AI industry pulled markets lower worldwide on Thursday, while oil prices hit their highest levels since May on worries about the war with Iran .
The S&P 500 fell 1.2% for its worst day since July, while the Nasdaq composite tumbled 2.6%. The weakness for tech stocks was so overwhelming that it masked strength for the rest of the US market, in which the majority of stocks actually rose. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 11 points, or less than 0.1%.
AI-related stocks have been swinging on worries that their boom may be under threat because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money to build datacenters and buy more AI chips. Concerns also remain that their prices shot too high following a years-long frenzy, even though companies in the industry continue to report growth.
Lam Research, whose equipment and services help make semiconductors, reported gains in profit and revenue for the summer that were slightly stronger than analysts expected, for example. Usually, that helps boost a stock’s price, but Lam Research’s tumbled 11.8%.
Other big tech stocks likewise fell following quarterly reports that included at least some encouraging nuggets.
Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent, lost 7% after reporting stronger revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, shedding tens of billions in market value, though its profit fell short. The company behind Facebook and Instagram also said it was creating a new class of stock to raise money to pay for AI investments and other expenses.
Tesla fell 3.1% after reporting a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected, though its revenue was weaker than forecast.
The global tide against AI stocks knocked Nvidia down 4.4%. Because the chip giant is the largest company on Wall Street by total value, movements for its stock carry more weight on the S&P 500 than any other, and it was the single strongest force pulling the index lower.
CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy Nvidia’s AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly shaky in recent weeks because of worries about its debt. It dropped 10.1%.
The weakness for AI and other tech stocks began in Asia, where indexes are full of players in the industry. South Korea’s Kospi tumbled 3.5%, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 3% and Japan’s Nikkei 225 sank 2.7%.
Also weighing on global stock markets was a jump in oil prices.
The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil leaped 4% to $113.17 after touching its highest level in five months. It’s shot up from less than $97 at the start of the month on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global energy industry to return to normal.
In Europe, France’s CAC 40 stock index fell to one of the continent’s sharpest losses with a drop of 1.4%. It has fewer tech stocks than Asian or US indexes, but it was hurt by another jump in yields for French government bonds.
Yields have been generally climbing there because of worries about the government’s big debt load and strained budget. Violent protests across France have raised pressure on the government to increase spending, which could add further to its debt.

Worries about big government debt are weighing on almost every developed economy in the world, including the United States. Such concerns, along with high inflation, signals of a still-strong US economy and other factors, have pushed yields in the US bond market recently to their highest levels in decades.
But US yields nevertheless fell sharply on Thursday in a signal that investors were buying US government bonds in search of something safer to own as AI stocks tumbled.
The yield on the 10-year treasury tumbled to 4.97% from 5.13% late on Wednesday and from more than 5.30% earlier this month. That’s a major move for the bond market.
Thursday’s drop in yields came even as another report suggested the US economy may be doing better than economists expected. It said fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, which could signal that layoffs remain low across the country.
That solid economy has helped US companies broadly to make bigger profits, which is what propelled the US stock market to a record high earlier this month despite the many worries tugging at it. Two out of every three stocks within the S&P 500 rose on Thursday, only to get drowned out by the drops for more influential tech stocks.
Procter & Gamble, Lockheed Martin and CSX were among the latest companies to join the list of those topping profit expectations for the summer, and gains for their stocks helped limit the market’s losses on Thursday.
CEO Shailesh Jejurikar said Procter & Gamble expected “geopolitical and economic challenges” to continue, but it stood by its forecasts for growth in revenue, profit and other measures for the full year. The stock price for the company behind the Crest, Olay and Oral-B brands rose 5.6%.
All told, the S&P 500 fell 93.74 points, to 7,663.43. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 11.89, to 52,867.98, and the Nasdaq composite tumbled 694.00, to 26,008.86.

articles.title_orig: Trump signs housing affordability executive order
articles.title_zh: Trump signs housing affordability executive order
articles.content_orig:
The White House is considering ordering Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and multiple federal agencies to implement a raft of policy changes aimed at lowering mortgage financing costs ahead of upcoming midterm elections, according to a draft executive order obtained by Scotsman Guide.
The proposed order would direct the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) and Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) — which oversee government-guaranteed mortgage programs — to unliterally lower mortgage rates on single-family loans using agency authorities.
Fannie and Freddie, according to the draft order, would also be directed to review their portfolios for borrowers eligible to have their mortgage insurance “cancelled proactively,” in keeping with safety and soundness expectations, their contractual obligations and growing collateral risks .
Mortgage servicers thus could be mandated by Fannie and Freddie, “to the extent permitted by law and operationally feasible, to notify borrowers promptly when mortgage insurance may be cancelled” and reduce and eliminate “unnecessary documentation requests, appraisal costs, and other administrative barriers to cancellation.”
The draft order reviewed by Scotsman Guide is subject to change — or may not be issued at all — but multiple industry sources who have seen the document said it may be issued by the White House as soon as Wednesday.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday.
Organized into five sections and containing a multitude of provisions , the draft executive order is titled “Decreasing Housing Costs for the American People.” It is unclear whether the range of directives in the order comply with existing mortgage laws and authorities of relevant federal agencies.
“Over the past two decades, many creditworthy Americans have been locked out of homeownership due to the rising costs associated with homeownership,” the draft order states as its purpose, citing “unnecessary” regulatory requirements and “outdated” origination processes that have increased closing costs and “made homeownership unaffordable.”
Just weeks out from hotly contested November midterm elections, Republican lawmakers in the Senate and House of Representatives are struggling to carry their water with voters as surveys favor Democrats to win back both chambers of Congress. Costs of living are voters’ primary concern , as they were during the presidential election in 2024 when Republicans won the White House and took control of both the House and Senate.
Perhaps nowhere are ongoing homebuying affordability challenges more visible than in mortgage rates now averaging more than 7%, compared to rates of around 6% in February. Elevated borrowing costs have amplified mortgage rate lock-in effects, given that two-thirds of existing borrowers have loans with rates under 5%.
Not only have elevated borrowing costs sidelined prospective buyers and slowed housing turnover to multidecade lows, but higher rates have also sapped the market of refinance demand .
Many borrowers have stretched their budgets in recent years to purchase a home at elevated mortgage rates — with the intention of lowering their monthly payments by refinancing when rates drop. But rates have only steadily risen since March and are projected to spend all of 2027 around current levels, according to economists at Fannie Mae and the Mortgage Bankers Association.
The draft order would authorize Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) Director Bill Pulte to consider significant expansion of a title insurance waiver pilot program for eligible refinances, with the aim of lowering closing costs on refinances in a range of new ways.
The FHFA did not respond to Scotsman Guide’s request for comment.
The title waiver pilot program began in 2024 and allowed for alternative title verification methods on certain refinance transactions. That includes removing geographic limitations, widening eligibility to borrowers with less than 20% equity and “certifying additional title-assessment providers to promote competition.”
The draft order also proposes “reducing or eliminating loan-level price adjustments” for eligible refinances and “waiving appraisals, income re-verification, and other documentation requirements for limited cash-out refinances that reduce the borrower’s monthly payment, where the Enterprise’s existing data support doing so.”
In lieu of appraisals, the order suggests Fannie and Freddie would “embrace innovative risk and value assessment technologies that incorporate Super Intelligence to drive down mortgage and homeownership costs,” using President Donald Trump’s preferred term for artificial intelligence.
“The Director shall require that cost savings resulting from the program be passed through to borrowers and that lenders inform borrowers of those savings,” the draft order states.
Taking a page out of Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh’s book, one section of the draft order would direct the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), Department of Commerce, VA and USDA to start a “task force” to standardize permitting and facilitate production of manufactured and factory-built housing.
That task force, which would be co-chaired by Pulte and HUD Secretary Scott Turner, would also evaluate under what existing laws federal grant funding “may be conditioned” on adoption of standardized permitting and licensing for factory-built housing at the state and local levels.

articles.title_orig: Meta’s deal to keep Zuckerberg in California adds fuel to wealth tax debate ahead of election
articles.title_zh: Meta’s deal to keep Zuckerberg in California adds fuel to wealth tax debate ahead of election
articles.content_orig:
In case there were any doubts, Mark Zuckerberg is staying in California.
Meta was apparently concerned enough that its founder and CEO might depart its home state that the company put in place a new stock plan that could help offset the burden of higher taxes should a billionaires tax, known as Proposition 40, pass on Election Day on Nov. 3.
The disclosure came in a filing on Wednesday that coincided with Meta's third-quarter earnings report, and represents a first among California's mega-cap tech companies. Zuckerberg, the sixth-richest person in the world, is one of the few among his peers to still reside in the state, along with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang .
Elon Musk and Michael Dell live in Texas, while Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' primary residence has always been elsewhere. Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin moved out of California ahead of the election and bought luxury homes in Florida, the same state that Oracle founder Larry Ellison officially calls home.
Prop. 40 would impose a 5% tax on Californians worth over $1 billion. Zuckerberg's net worth is currently about $225 billion.
"If the California wealth tax is enacted and Mr. Zuckerberg becomes liable for a tax payment, Mr. Zuckerberg would effectively be paying to serve as the Company's chief executive officer while residing in California," the filing said, noting the CEO's "salary of only $1 each year."
Meta said in the filing that Zuckerberg committed to remaining in California for eight years, "unless there are material unforeseen circumstances that would render it prudent or advisable for Mr. Zuckerberg to reside elsewhere."
The company created a new class of non-voting Class C common stock to take effect in January. Zuckerberg will essentially be granted a portion of the new stock via a dividend. He will be able to "immediately sell or transfer up to 20%" of the shares he's granted "for any reason, including so that he may pay his potential tax liability under California Proposition 40, if enacted into law, without affecting his majority voting control," the filing said.
"There were many driving factors that led the board and special committee to approve the Class C shares, and it would be misleading to attribute it to any single reason," Meta told CNBC in a statement.
The tech industry, by and large, has been unified in its objection to the ballot measure.
In addition to the Google co-founders, a number of big-name techies have put spending into opposing Prop. 40. They include former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, Stripe CEO Patrick Collison, venture investor Peter Thiel and DoorDash CEO Tony Xu, according to various media reports based on campaign filings.
Collison and Xu are members of Meta's board of directors while Thiel left the company's board in 2022, having served since 2005.
Brin told The New York Times in April he fled the Soviet Union with his family in 1979, and said, "I don't want California to end up in the same place."
Huang, however, recently told CBS Sunday Morning that it would be a "privilege" to pay the tax. Huang is just behind Zuckerberg in Forbes' billionaire ranking , with a net worth of $185 billion.
Although Prop. 40 advocates, including Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., have been urging voters to pass the ballot measure , recent polling has suggested that it may fail to garner the majority support required to make it law. A recent Citrin-Politico poll showed 46% are in favor of the measure compared with 43% who oppose it.
Meta, with the help of a special committee, views Zuckerberg as key to the company's future and its efforts to become a major player in artificial intelligence, according to the filing. In particular, the company said it doesn't want to jeopardize Zuckerberg's close working arrangement with the Meta Superintelligence Labs , which is led by AI chief Alexandr Wang .
"The Special Committee believes that Mr. Zuckerberg's talent and leadership have been crucial to our growth, strategy, and stability since our inception, and the Special Committee wants that to continue," the filing said.
Although Meta considered the possibility of issuing Class A common stock to help raise funds, the filing noted that Zuckerberg made clear "that he would not support a significant equity financing that would have the effect of reducing his voting power in the Company."
Instead, the new stock incentive will help Meta receive "critical equity capital without impacting Mr. Zuckerberg's voting power and the unique and creative vision and exceptional management abilities which helped to deliver the long-term value as noted above," the filing said.

Beijing offers to remove restrictions on a German supplier to chipmaking giant ASML in exchange for the EU delisting Chinese firm Yusha
Diplomats from the EU’s 27 member states were pressured this week to lift sanctions on Yusha Group, a Chinese textiles manufacturer accused of selling sensitive European technology to Russian buyers.
In exchange, Beijing has pledged that the company will refrain from shipping banned items to Russian military-linked buyers. It will also remove German company Sindlhauser Materials from its own export controls list, according to multiple sources familiar with the affair.
The unusual quid pro quo – the product of high-wire negotiations at the top level of EU and Chinese politics – is designed to protect the supply chain of Europe’s most valuable technology company, Dutch-based ASML, of which Sindlhauser is a reported supplier.

articles.title_orig: Moderna’s Stock Plummets After Cancer-Vaccine Data Shared on Social Media
articles.title_zh: Moderna’s Stock Plummets After Cancer-Vaccine Data Shared on Social Media
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Two months ago, Moderna's ( MRNA ) melanoma vaccine handed the stock its best day ever. Now leaked results from the same trial have handed it its biggest intraday drop on record.
The stock fell as much as 26% before closing down more than 17%. That's still its worst day since Aug. 20, the session right after its best day.
More than $17 billion in market value has vanished as details from the late-stage trial circulated ahead of their official debut . Merck ( MRK ), Moderna's partner on the vaccine, confirmed the results came out early. The full data is set for release Saturday at Europe's biggest cancer conference, in Madrid.
The leaked numbers are still good. The personalized vaccine, paired with Merck's blockbuster Keytruda, reportedly cut the risk of the cancer returning or death by 42%. An earlier, smaller trial showed 49%, though it used different patients, so it isn't a direct comparison. The bigger issue is how much the stock had already run, nearly quadrupling from mid-August to Wednesday.
Merck fell nearly 4% at its low before paring more than half the drop. The vaccine is central to Moderna's story, but it's just an add-on for Merck.
The rest of healthcare is rallied. Eli Lilly ( LLY ) is added more than $33 billion in market value, about twice what Moderna lost. Johnson & Johnson ( JNJ ) and Pfizer ( PFE ) rose, too.
The iShares Biotechnology ETF ( IBB ) and SPDR S&P Biotech ETF ( XBI ) were only modestly lower, roughly in step with the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ).
On Aug. 19, Moderna rocketed 177% to close at $174.38 after the company said the trial met its goals. It kept climbing from there, and on Wednesday, it posted its highest close since December 2021.
Thursday's low came within 4% of that August close before buyers stepped in. A sustained break below $174 would put $116 in focus. That's where trading opened on the record day.
Watch Saturday's full data, especially how lower-risk patients fared.

articles.title_orig: Russian missiles pound Kyiv as Moscow says over 800 Ukrainian drones downed
articles.title_zh: Russian missiles pound Kyiv as Moscow says over 800 Ukrainian drones downed
articles.content_orig:
Estimated read time: 5-6 minutes
KYIV, Ukraine — Russia bombarded Kyiv with ballistic missiles in an hourslong nighttime barrage, while the Russian military said Thursday that its air defenses intercepted over 800 drones fired by Ukraine at Moscow and other cities.
At least four people were killed in Ukraine and dozens of others were wounded, officials said, in the attacks that began only hours after Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed "in principle" on Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations between Russia, Ukraine and the United States.
"Russia has not changed the way it wages this war, and it is taking no steps that would signal a genuine desire to end it," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said after the latest large-scale barrage.
Putin's consent came in talks in St. Petersburg with President Donald Trump's envoy, Steve Witkoff, who had spoken of a "new momentum" toward peace after meeting Tuesday with Zelenskyy in Norway. No date was set for the tripartite talks.
Representatives of the three countries held rounds of "technical" talks in the United Arab Emirates and Switzerland in January and February, seeking to lay the groundwork for detailed negotiations. But they reported little progress beyond exchanges of prisoners of war. Russia and Ukraine remain far apart in their terms for stopping the fighting despite U.S. efforts.
Zelenskyy says only a meeting of leaders can end the deadlock.
Russia's aerial attacks hit 12 regions of Ukraine overnight, killing at least four people and wounding scores of others, including five children, Zelenskyy said on social media Thursday.
Two women aged 50 and 60 were killed and dozens of others wounded in a Russian strike on a market in Lozova, in Ukraine's northeastern Kharkiv region, said Oleh Syniehubov, head of the regional military administration. Another person was killed in other strikes on Kharkiv, the State Emergency Service said.
The Ukrainian capital endured a noisy night as 21 ballistic missiles came in three waves, Zelenskyy said, smashing apartment buildings, energy facilities, a railway station and the Kyiv subway system, shopping malls and businesses. One person was killed in Kyiv.
The Russian attack on Kyiv included three ballistic missiles carrying cluster munitions — bombs that open in the air and release scores of smaller bomblets, Zelenskyy said.
Ukrainians are bracing for the bitterly cold months ahead as the recent escalation in Russian attacks targets the power grid to deny civilians heat, light and running water. Ukraine says Russia is stockpiling ballistic missiles for an annual campaign Ukrainians describe as "weaponizing winter."
Since Oct. 11, Russia has launched 170 strikes on Ukraine's critical energy facilities, Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian leader has pleaded with Washington to supply more Patriot air defense ammunition to stop the ballistic missiles, and to heap more sanctions on Russia to pressure Moscow to pursue peace.
Instead, Trump has agreed with Putin to import diesel from Russia and waived heavy sanctions on Moscow, while U.S. officials say Patriot ammunition is in short supply.
"Russia is clearly taking advantage of the slowdown in air defense supplies from our partners," Zelenskyy said. "It is equally clear that when some partners ease the pressure on Russia, it only reinforces Putin's belief that his goals are within reach."
Western analysts say Putin wants to cut out Europe and Kyiv and negotiate Ukraine's future directly with Washington. The Trump administration has also disparaged Europe.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Thursday that Putin had received an invitation to attend the G20 summit in Miami in December but hasn't yet decided whether to go.
"The American administration is doing a lot to help a peaceful settlement," Peskov told reporters. "European capitals are doing nothing to promote a peaceful resolution, and they are doing a great deal to provoke the further escalation of fighting."
Witkoff, the Trump envoy who met with Putin in St. Petersburg on Wednesday, was harshly criticized in Ukraine and in the U.S. for praising the Russian leader as a "humanitarian" for ordering the release of a retired American teacher who was imprisoned on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine.
Assassination attempts against Putin's foes — routinely denied by the Kremlin — have been common during his decades in power. And as the five-year anniversary of Russia's all-out invasion of its neighbor approaches, aerial strikes have killed thousands of civilians and hundreds of thousands of soldiers.
The latest "brutal" Russian attacks demonstrate "what Russian 'humanism' truly sounds like," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on social media. "Appeasement, servility, and flattery will not stop this war. Only strength will."
Russia's Defense Ministry said that air defenses overnight downed 808 Ukrainian drones, with two people reported wounded.
Moscow's Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that 630 of the drones were fired toward the Russian capital between late Wednesday and early Thursday. Moscow airports temporarily restricted air traffic overnight.
The Russian military hit the facilities involved in making and storing drones and cruise missiles and transport infrastructure in Kyiv in overnight strikes, the Defense Ministry said. Infrastructure in the southern port of Odesa and vessels used for the Ukrainian armed forces were also hit, it said.
In other developments, the bodies of 252 people, said by Russia to be Ukrainian soldiers, were returned to Ukraine in an exchange, Ukraine's Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War said Thursday.
Russia received 25 bodies of Russian soldiers, Russian lawmaker Shamsail Saraliyev, a member of a parliamentary coordination group overseeing the exchanges, told the RBC news outlet.

Two months ago, Moderna's ( MRNA ) melanoma vaccine handed the stock its best day ever. Now leaked results from the same trial have handed it its biggest intraday drop on record.
The stock fell as much as 26% before closing down more than 17%. That's still its worst day since Aug. 20, the session right after its best day.
More than $17 billion in market value has vanished as details from the late-stage trial circulated ahead of their official debut . Merck ( MRK ), Moderna's partner on the vaccine, confirmed the results came out early. The full data is set for release Saturday at Europe's biggest cancer conference, in Madrid.
The leaked numbers are still good. The personalized vaccine, paired with Merck's blockbuster Keytruda, reportedly cut the risk of the cancer returning or death by 42%. An earlier, smaller trial showed 49%, though it used different patients, so it isn't a direct comparison. The bigger issue is how much the stock had already run, nearly quadrupling from mid-August to Wednesday.
Merck fell nearly 4% at its low before paring more than half the drop. The vaccine is central to Moderna's story, but it's just an add-on for Merck.
The rest of healthcare is rallied. Eli Lilly ( LLY ) is added more than $33 billion in market value, about twice what Moderna lost. Johnson & Johnson ( JNJ ) and Pfizer ( PFE ) rose, too.
The iShares Biotechnology ETF ( IBB ) and SPDR S&P Biotech ETF ( XBI ) were only modestly lower, roughly in step with the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ).
On Aug. 19, Moderna rocketed 177% to close at $174.38 after the company said the trial met its goals. It kept climbing from there, and on Wednesday, it posted its highest close since December 2021.
Thursday's low came within 4% of that August close before buyers stepped in. A sustained break below $174 would put $116 in focus. That's where trading opened on the record day.
Watch Saturday's full data, especially how lower-risk patients fared.

articles.content_orig:
Treasury yields fell sharply on Thursday, with investors turning to safe havens amid a steep sell-off in stocks driven by concerns around the artificial intelligence trade and surging oil prices.
The benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury yield — used to price mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — slid more than 17 basis points to 4.972%, the first time below 5% since Sept. 23. The yield saw its biggest one-day decline since March 10, 2023.
The yield on the 2-year Treasury note , which closely tracks short-term Federal Reserve rate policy, tumbled more than 16 basis points to 4.659%. The yield on longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasury — most sensitive to geopolitical developments — was more than 14 basis points lower at 5.296%.
One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.
"It is a flight to safety," said Mitch Goldberg, president of ClientFirst Strategy. "People are all of a sudden terrified of the amount of bond issuance by AI-related companies. They see the rates going up and people want to hold on to something that they think will be there at maturity."
Others on Wall Street also sought to explain the turnaround in bond prices.
"For the first time in a while, Treasurys are enjoying haven status," said Larry Holzenthaler, senior portfolio manager for fixed income at Catalyst Funds. "You have weakness in tech, an escalation of risk in the Middle East and higher oil. On a relative basis Treasurys start to look like the safe place to hide again in the short term."
The reversal in bonds this week emerged as questions persisted about the billions being spent to build artificial intelligence networks.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC Thursday that while demand for neoclouds is " off the charts ," capital was scarce. Neoclouds are a specialized cloud computing providers that focus on high-performance tech infrastructure designed specifically for artificial intelligence.
This week's rebound in Treasury prices marks a turnaround from earlier this month, when 10- and 30-year yields reached their highest levels in more than two decades amid investor concern over inflation and high energy prices.
Above 5%, however, attitudes began to shift and yields suddenly starting looking like an attractive entry point, compensating even for the risk of inflation above 3%.
Tensions in the Middle East added to risk-off behavior Thursday. Oil prices moved sharply higher, with West Texas Intermediate futures closing up 2.39% at $99.47 per barrel. Brent crude futures, the global price benchmark, jumped 4%, rising to $113.17 a barrel.
Higher energy prices followed a New York Times report, citing unnamed U.S. officials, that the U.S. and Israel are considering resuming strikes on Iran in a "short but intensive" operation following the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
"You always look for one risk point, and there isn't really just one at the moment, which makes it a little bit more challenging," said Gregory Faranello, head of U.S. macro strategy at South Street Securities. "But if I had to take one of those and say what's most important right now, it has to be what's going on geopolitically."
"The consumer is clearly getting pinched here in the U.S., so it becomes tricky for central bankers" setting monetary policy going forward, he said. If energy prices "stay elevated, it could force the Fed's hand to do even more, which certainly wouldn't be wouldn't be a good thing for the bond market."

Oh sure, SpaceX’s credit risk is pretty high because it’s about to borrow another $40 billion to spend on Nvidia chips , but who cares about that? SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss a merger!
The degree to which you find this merger compelling likely has to do with the degree to which you believe Elon Musk about wanting to go to Mars, or “spread the light of consciousness,” as he put it in this week’s SpaceX earnings call (and earlier S-1). Now, a reasonably informed person knows that we don’t have the technology — or, frankly, even the raw information to build the technology — in order to support human life in space. So that means robots. But a lag between Earth and the Moon or Mars makes for difficulty in controlling the robots. So having artificially intelligent robots who can make decisions on their own with minimal supervision from Earth is the next sci-fi logic step.
“There’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software.”
If you believe Musk’s story, the technology we are talking about is being developed through self-driving cars (Tesla), LLMs (SpaceX), and humanoid robots (Tesla), all of which require data centers (SpaceX). Conveniently, we have just had earnings for both companies. On the other hand, if you view Mars as a useful fiction Musk uses to explain his antics in public, well, there’s a lot of money and a lot of control Musk gets from the merger.
Musk said on the recent SpaceX earnings call that “there’s a lot of merit to combining” SpaceX and Tesla. Why? “There’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software.” But artificial intelligence — ah, excuse me, super intelligence software isn’t the business SpaceX is really in right now. In its Q3 earnings on Tuesday, SpaceX reported $7.56 billion in revenue from the artificial intelligence — sorry, sorry, super intelligence division. The subcategory “SI solutions & infrastructure revenues” — which I think is Grok, Cursor, and the neocloud business wrapped together — jumped to $7 billion, or more than three times what it was last quarter. Now some of this was getting Cursor stapled on , which added $608 million in revenue. Most of the rest of that $7 billion was likely renting out compute to Anthropic and Google; Grok is probably contributing less, says Gil Luria, an analyst at DA Davidson.
At first blush, this may look comparable to the revenue of a company like Anthropic, whose leaked S-1 shows the company had $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of this year from its frontier models. But SpaceX’s AI business looks more like CoreWeave than Anthropic. While we are told in the press release there was “increased Grok adoption across enterprise customers and consumers,” that number wasn’t broken out from bare-metal revenue. And if Musk wanted to brag about it, he would.
As for Tesla, which released Q3 results on Wednesday, its earnings sucked — a second consecutive quarter of declining profits. That’s because Musk is apparently not especially interested in normal cars anymore. Instead, Tesla is focusing on robots and, I guess, self-driving taxis. (There was also a Roadster hopping car demo recently , but that’s not going into production for a couple years, it’s very expensive, and Tesla cannot guarantee it will be delivered .) Musk did not elaborate on his comments about the merger on the Tesla call.
SpaceX and Tesla have some tie-ups already; SpaceX, for instance, bought $131 million of the low-selling Cybertrucks from Tesla. It has, in the past, held Tesla bonds. More crucially, the companies have also announced two AI — fuck it, we’re just sticking with AI — projects together: Terafab and Macrohard.
Terafab is the chip-making venture that Musk intends to build in Texas and run to supply himself with chips; Intel is partnered, kinda, with Musk to develop the technology. Macrohard is, uh, an AI project that lets people simulate software already made by Microsoft . At least, I think that’s what it’s supposed to be. Typing the name of the latter makes me pray for the asteroid to hit us all right now, so perhaps it’s fortunate that we haven’t heard much about it since the announcement in March.

Intel’s Thomas Hannaford didn’t immediately respond to my emails asking if anything had been signed in the interim.
On this week’s call with SpaceX investors, Musk claimed the Terafab will reach volume production in the second half of 2028 . When an analyst on the call asked if Musk had placed orders for machines needed to make cutting-edge equipment, Musk did not answer.
Companies often are doing more privately than they announce publicly, so I do not view the S-1 filing as fully definitive. But Macrohard isn’t mentioned in the last 10Q. Neither is Terafab.

Sometimes he’s very excited about rockets, and sometimes he’s very excited about Dogecoin and sometimes he’s really into Grok and sometimes he thinks about cars. But you notice that one way or the other he’s been thinking about cars a lot less lately.

IRVINE, Calif. — KFC dumped PepsiCo last week, but its sister chain Taco Bell announced Thursday it's keeping the Mountain Dew Baja Blast maker on for another decade.
The Taco Bell deal is a much-needed win for PepsiCo, whose business has had rough few weeks. Not only did it lose its longstanding contract with KFC to rival Coca-Cola , but its drink business in North America is also in a slump.
The company reported a 2% decline for its North America beverage unit during its most recent quarter, and its CEO Ramon Laguarta bluntly said on its earnings call that it's "not competing well in soft drinks," including newly acquired Poppi brand.
Losing the KFC contract is a blow for PepsiCo, considering it once owned the fried chicken chain. But keeping Taco Bell is a bigger deal, since the latter has generated $17 billion in U.S. systemwide sales last year compared to KFC's roughly $5 billion. (Both chains are owned by Yum! Brands.)
Taco Bell and PepsiCo said in a statement that the two will continue collaborating on new beverages and foods until 2036, including upcoming new flavors for their Doritos Locos Tacos. It also noted that the Baja Blast drink has become a $1 billion brand.
As food prices rise and consumers look to cut back, the beverage category is a key growth area for Taco Bell and other fast food chains.
Taco Bell is aggressively expanding its beverage sales aiming to generate $5 billion in revenue by 2030. Last year, the chain released a lineup of "Refrescas" drinks aimed at attracting consumers searching for a beverage between meals. Further expansion will come from developing new Baja Blast options with Pepsi, including a limited-time pink lemonade with singer Olivia Rodrigo.
"Taco Bell's Baja Blast lineup has often been a key differentiator for the brand, and leaning into product exclusives can help drive visitation to quick service restaurant chains," Elizabeth Lafontaine, director of research at location analytics firm Placer.ai, previously told CNN.
"Especially as the industry faces steeper competition and consumers who are on the hunt for more value from fast food offerings," she added.
Taco Bell and PepsiCo said in a statement that they plan to stay ahead on "emerging beverage trends across crafted, functional and energy beverages, including energy offerings designed to appeal to Gen Z consumers and unlock new morning and afternoon occasions."
Taco Bell has been a bright spot in the fast food industry, but saw a traffic decline over the summer due to a cyclosporasis outbreak that was linked to lettuce served at a number of restaurants. The company will give a fuller view of the sales impact when it releases earnings next month.

articles.title_zh: Hegseth bans DoD personnel from using nonpublic info to bet on U.S. military operations
articles.content_orig:
Washington — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has banned Defense Department personnel from using nonpublic information to bet on U.S. military operations, according to a memorandum obtained by CBS News.
In the Oct. 20 message to senior Pentagon leadership and combatant commanders, Hegseth said the prohibition would apply to classified and unclassified information and specifically includes prediction markets such as Polymarket and Kalshi, which are named in the memo.
The defense secretary warned that financial transactions on prediction markets could expose sensitive military movements to foreign adversaries and endanger American troops.
"Make no mistake why this matters. Our enemies watch movements in these markets," Hegseth wrote. "When an American Service member, intelligence professional, or other Department civilian engages in a financial transaction on a military outcome, they create a signal."
Hegseth warned that foreign intelligence services could analyze betting activity to anticipate American military movements, targets and timing of an operation. The memorandum said violations could result in administrative disciplinary or criminal action under federal law or the Uniform Code of Military Justice, the laws and regulations governing the U.S. military.
The directive follows growing scrutiny of service members participating in military-related prediction markets. In April, a U.S. Special Forces soldier involved in the military operation that captured Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro was arrested after allegedly betting on Maduro's removal from office before news of the raid was made public.
Federal investigators believe U.S. Army Master Sgt. Gannon Ken Van Dyke made bets of more than $33,000 on the prediction market Polymarket within hours of President Trump's announcement in January that Maduro had been captured. The bets resulted in winnings of more than $409,000.
The soldier entered a not guilty plea in New York federal court.
