French President Emmanuel Macron, whose popularity ratings (at around 18 percent) are well below Trump’s, exited Paris yesterday for the Middle East, even as some neighborhoods of major French cities were still smoking. Supposedly, he is on a mission to bring down fuel prices. Bonne chance to that.
The French mess is best understood in three dimensions that are all connected—the social, the economic, and the political. Socially, the protests, which caught the government by surprise in their ferocity, are mainly symptoms. The most severe riots since the famous events of 1968 began with high school students, who are ostensibly fed up with tattered schools and inadequate materials. But what they are really despairing about is the absence of life chances and hope.
Much of this protest is centered in the French banlieues —the suburbs . In France, where the social meaning of suburb is the opposite of America’s, the banlieues are where the government stashed immigrants and the local poor in massive housing projects that are bleak social failures, while the affluent live in chic city arrondissements .
This story first appeared in our free Today on TAP newsletter, a weekday email featuring commentary on the daily news from Prospect reporters.
No paywall, no programmatic ads — just the reporting. Unsubscribe anytime. Submitting your email signs you up for Today on TAP, our weekday afternoon newsletter.
This social failure is hardly a secret. Several recent hit French films are about seemingly unteachable insolent students and idealistic but quickly burnt-out teachers, beginning with the 2008 classic Entre Les Murs . In the popular TV series, Marseille , starring the great warhorse actor Gérard Depardieu as the mayor, kids in the housing projects do violent errands for the local Mafia.
And it isn’t just students who are disaffected. Just about everyone is pissed at one grievance or another. That’s why the protests spread. The French riots are reminiscent of the old Irish joke in which a man in a pub observes a brawl break out and inquires, “Is this a private fight or can anyone get into it?”
France’s welfare state has reached it limits to compensate for an economy that works only for the rich.
The second, and related, dimension is economic. The French economic model is failing the citizenry, and its failure is a variation of what is occurring throughout the West.
The turn to global neoliberalism since the 1980s has not increased economic performance, but widened inequality. The lackluster growth has put increased pressure on the French welfare state, which is relatively generous. But the welfare state has reached its limits to compensate for an economy that works only for the rich.
As French deficits and debts have increased, the global bond market has raised government borrowing costs, exacerbating the fiscal stress. Interestingly, it is considered a crisis that the French ten-year government bond just hit an interest rate of 5 percent . In the U.S., the ten-year bond sailed past 5 percent weeks ago. But France, as a medium-sized economy, is more dependent on the bond market than the U.S. is.
Macron, the ultimate in technocratic leaders, has tried to trim costs, most recently with a 43 billion euro cut in public spending in his proposed 2026-2027 budget, which includes an increase in the retirement age and cuts in health and other social spending. But these proposed cuts, which are unlikely to be enacted, have only made him more detested.
Politically, these multiple crises, punctuated by protests that in places turned violent, demonstrated the collapse of the political center, and energized the far left and especially the far right. With presidential elections set for April 2027, in two rounds, Marine Le Pen of the Rassemblement National (National Rally) is the front-runner . On the far left, Jean-Luc Mélenchon of La France Insoumise (France Unbowed) cheered on the protests.
Polls show Mélenchon running second, well behind Le Pen. If the final round is Le Pen versus Mélenchon, Le Pen almost certainly wins and by a wide margin. Other candidates on the moderate left and moderate right splinter the rest of the vote.
One outside chance of denying the presidency to Le Pen would be if Raphaël Glucksmann, the nominee of the Socialist Party, continues to gain ground and edges out Mélenchon to face Le Pen in the final round. The latest polls show Le Pen at 36 percent, Mélenchon with 16.5 percent, and Glucksmann 13.5 percent. On the center-right, former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe draws about the same share as Glucksmann.
While the far-left Mélenchon could not defeat Le Pen in the final, Glucksmann or Philippe might well do it. But for that to happen, one would have to withdraw and throw their support to the other—a most un-French sacrifice for the greater good.
The French gains for the far left and the far right are a variant of what is occurring all over Europe, as the center has utterly failed to deliver prosperity and opportunity to ordinary working people and cultural issues have backfired on the socially tolerant moderate left.
In The New York Times, the estimable Steven Erlanger has a smart explainer piece on this dynamic. Complementing his own excellent analysis, Erlanger quotes the Nobel laureate MIT economist Daron Acemoglu pointing out that the traditional moderate left got sidetracked with elite cultural issues and ignored its working-class base. “The centerpiece has to be creating jobs and wage growth and career paths for people without college degrees and diverse skills,” Acemoglu told Erlanger in an interview.
As we used to say in my grade school, No shit, Dick Tracy. I can’t resist adding that when writers in The American Prospect , or our friends at the Economic Policy Institute, keep pointing this out (over decades), it’s not a story. When a prominent mainstream economist finally figures it out, it’s worth a Nobel.

Concerns have swirled over the access that consumers are increasingly entrusting to AI agents. Now, security services are trying to catch up.
Password manager 1Password on Thursday launched a new tool by which users can allow agents to log into their personal accounts on their behalf, without the agent ever having access to a user’s credentials.
The new platform, dubbed 1Password for Agents , accomplishes this by creating a system of communication between the agent, the user, and the password manager. When an agent attempts to log in on a user’s behalf, a unique digital key is sent to 1Password to confirm the agent’s digital identity. The user is then sent an alert about the login attempt and can personally confirm the request. 1Password then signs in the agent, filling in the credentials on the digital assistant’s behalf, which allows it to log in and complete whatever task is at hand.
1Password for Agents allows users to choose their agent of choice — whether that’s Claude Duet from Anthropic, OpenAI’s Dots or ChatGPT Work, Grok Bot, Meta’s Muse, or agents from Town, which is an AI assistant startup. The company says it is working with other companies to expand the service.
“Handing over a password, secret, or credential is a common shortcut to an agent, but can leave people with sensitive information in places they can no longer control as a copy gets saved for the next time,” the company said in a blog post . “1Password for Agents gives people a trusted way to delegate tasks to personal AI agents while keeping control of the passwords, secrets, and credentials those tasks require.”
Online agentic activity has increasingly unsettled major institutions. Indeed, 1Password’s new platform is launching on the same day that Axios reports that U.S. banks have begun to detect agentic activity inside user accounts.
This isn’t necessarily a case of rogue agents pilfering accounts but, rather, an example of how consumers are increasingly allowing automated services to act on their behalf, including on financial matters. However, the potential for agent-related problems is still large. The big issue appears to be that most banks cannot tell if the agentic activity is tied to user requests or not.
Bankers interviewed by the outlet described the situation as “horrifying,” and a Chase spokesperson interviewed by Axios additionally told the outlet that customers “should not give their usernames and passwords to anyone.”

The California Highway Patrol’s statement to media outlets says it reviewed video of the accident from the Tesla’s dashcam, which “showed the Tesla’s brakes being applied as the vehicle steered to the left in an effort to avoid the pedestrian [...] Despite these evasive actions, the right front portion of the Tesla struck the individual.”
According to the Chronicle , authorities believe at least one other vehicle struck the pedestrian after the Tesla, but other than the Tesla driver, who stopped and remained at the scene, no other drivers stopped. The CHP Solano Area office is asking that anyone who witnessed the accident or has any information contact them.

After that incident, CHP warned drivers that “Despite its name, full self-driving is not fully autonomous. Design platform Canva released its first image generation model, called Canva Craft, developed by its research team to compete with same-category models from Google, OpenAI, ByteDance, and Meta.
The company said its model works in two stages. In the first stage, it interprets users’ prompts and creates a plan with details like spatial relationships of elements, relative scale, visual hierarchy, and information for text generation. In the second stage, its model generates an image of up to 2K resolution in a possible 30 different aspect ratios for various platforms.
Canva said that this approach allows it to create images with accurate details of objects and legible text. Plus, users would be able to make precise edits without changing other parts of the image.
The company noted that rather than using photographs, it used designs to train this model using human-designed templates from Canva’s library, including posters, social posts, presentations, infographics, menus, and typography-rich layouts.
That means images generated with Canva Craft could be converted into layered designs using Canva Magic, the company’s image-to-design transformer. Last year, the platform released its own model that understands designs and layers .
Canva Craft is available on the company’s platform to all users, who can access the model from the Dream Lab tab. The model will also be available through the Canva API. Plus, the company plans to support image generation in third-party chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini through Canva’s MCP.
Canva has used a bunch of image models for generation in its platform, so it’s likely that the new models will help save API costs for the company. It said that besides costs, the new model also allows the platform to have better quality and speed control.
In 2024, Canva acquired media generation platform Leonardo.ai . It said that the researchers from Leonardo contributed to the new image model.
Canva said that it is developing two cost-efficient versions of the model, called Craftfast and Craft-ultrafast, which will be released soon.
The company was on track for $4 billion in revenue last year . However, it cut its growth forecast for 2026 , causing its valuation to reportedly plummet from $42 billion to $35 billion , according to external analysts.

articles.title_zh: OpenAI makes its Jev competitor widely available as decision model competition heats up
articles.content_orig:
Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.
Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.
OpenAI made its Decisions API model widely available to users for the first time, entering the market for fast, cheap intelligence that recently made TypeSafe, a startup founded by a former researcher at the frontier lab, a $7.6 billion company .
TypeSafe’s Jev model created a category for deep learning models that act as super classifiers: Given a set of options, they can quickly make choices and offer a confidence rating in their decision. Software developers quickly found that these decision or System One models could replace LLMs in a variety of workflows, operating more quickly and a at dramatically lower cost.
Nikunj Handa, the product lead for OpenAI’s APIs, told TechCrunch that his colleagues saw Jev and said “wow, we we have like a million use cases for this.” Handa’s team sprinted to offer their own version: Rather than building a specifically calibrated decision model, the team took ChatGPT Luna and reconfigured it to speed up the inference and lower the cost.
“The big unlock with Decisions API has been the speed, shrinking things from one to three seconds to 100, 120, 180 milliseconds,” Handa said. “In the future, we may sort of like have specific training to make our models like even better in these ways. But right now, it’s just plain old Luna that gets the job done.”
Announced at the company’s developer day on September 29, the Decisions API became available to all customers on Thursday. OpenAI added new voice and visual modalities to the public version, and worked to ensure lower latency in regions around the world by targeting its inference resources geographically.
In initial trials with customers like Box, Datadog, Ramp, and Speak, engineers used the API to replace OpenAI’s LLMs with higher throughput. Andrew Hsu, the CTO at Speak, which builds AI language tutors, said the Decisions API allowed the company to cut the time between actions from 1.4 seconds to .13 seconds. OpenAI also used the product to improve their Dots voice assistant’s responsiveness.
Still, it’s not clear exactly what makes a good decision model, other than “it works for you” — optimization across intelligence, cost, calibration, and speed seems to differ by workload. TypeSafe CEO Diogo Almeida distrusts benchmarks and urges people to trial the models in their own work, but even TypeSafe released its own rankings last week alongside the release of its latest Jev model, which includes new features including support for images and smart-if statements.
Public benchmarks like the AIM System One Index and the Artificial Analysis Decision Index tend to favor D1 Ultra, a new decision model that Liquid released last week, and Base Lab’s Elephant-1. The latest Jev model remains competitive on both indices, in seventh and third, with OpenAI’s Decision Model falling eighth and fourteenth, respectively. However, TypeSafe’s offerings are, for now, the most widely-queried on OpenRouter.
The most fun Jev benchmark, however, is JevMan , a benchmark where decision models play PacMan; the latest Jev model tops that ranking. Felix Wunderlich, the chief growth officer at Opper AI, which built the benchmark, said the classic game “is an interesting test because of its nonstop stream of quick, high-stakes decisions. At every junction the model must decide where to go in a few hundred milliseconds.”
Where OpenAI’s arguably more capable model may have an advantage is in multi-modality—for image classification, “Luna is extremely powerful and has been showing better calibrations,” Handa told TechCrunch, adding that OpenAI customers want the Decisions API to be more flexible about using images as outputs as well.
Handa also saw further increases in speed enabling new use cases: “Can we get this to something like you know 60 milliseconds, and then you could imagine like an API like call like for every single frame in like a video?”
As these offerings get faster and cheaper, we can expect them to live up to Jev’s namesake, an economist who explained how using a resource more efficiently makes it more ubiquitous. Or, as Handa sees it, there will be an expanding “crazy set of use cases” that were hiding in plain sight until the decision models revealed them.

The most dangerous Chinese technologies don’t look like weapons. A cellular module the size of a quarter, buried inside a larger machine. A robot dog built for search and rescue. Biotech research aimed at lifesaving cures. Beijing is turning all of them into instruments of military power. U.S. national security policy must catch up.

While China has become adept at turning emerging technology into military advantage, many U.S. national security tools were built for a world where the line between commercial and military technology was clearer.

articles.title_zh: News | Rising rates derail CBRE's real estate deal momentum
articles.content_orig:
The company saw strong growth in facilities management and critical infrastructure services, executives said Thursday, but project management growth dipped as corporations cut real estate spending.
CBRE’s revenue grew 13% year over year to $11.5 billion, the company reported . On a net revenue basis, its project management business grew 11%, driven in part by growth in infrastructure projects. That segment “is a very large part of our project management business [and] more than [offsets] the slowdown in real estate,” Giamartino said.
CBRE’s critical infrastructure services business — which includes network infrastructure, mechanical, engineering and plumbing projects and facilities management for data centers — is expected to generate nearly $4.5 billion of revenue in 2027, according to Sulentic.
Its acquisition of a global IT infrastructure company, Onnec Group Limited, will help drive the growth, said Sulentic, adding that even if data center growth in the U.S. eases, growth is expected to increase in other countries.
“Our acquisition of Onnec, which we announced today, fits within this line of business,” Sulentic said.
The $610 million cash deal provides CBRE with technical capabilities related to design, deployment and maintenance of network, fiber and data center infrastructure, a specialty area that’s critical to data centers, per a release Tuesday .
If the business achieves the entirety of the deal’s earn-outs, the deal will end up costing CBRE a little over $1 billion, which the firm is using as an incentive to continue to generate strong growth, Giamartino said.
The firm expects to close the acquisition by the end of the year, said Giamartino, noting that if the acquisition were included, the firm’s critical infrastructure services business would have generated approximately $3 billion in revenue over the past 12 months.
Although the company’s enterprise facilities management posted solid growth, it’s facing pressure from a handful of problematic accounts. “That’s happened from time to time over the years,” Sulentic said. “The market gets frothy, it gets more and more competitive and you … end up with some broker hires or outsourcing or enterprise accounts that don’t have the characteristics you would want.”
CBRE’s project management revenue slowed, up 3% year over year, as corporate clients acted more conservatively due to uncertainty in the economy, Sulentic said.
“We do a lot of work for big tech clients that have moved their spending away from … traditional legacy real estate-type investment into infrastructure, critical infrastructure, data centers,” he said. “I think you’re seeing some of that.” The firm also saw “a little bit of concentration slowdown in healthcare,” he said.
“What we really need is for rates to stabilize,” Giamartino said. “The volatility and the uncertainty is what’s driving a pause or a hold or even delaying deals to 2027. We expect that stability to come in the back half of next year….  Of course, if that doesn’t come or things change, the results will be different.”
In the U.S., leasing revenue rose 4%, supported by industrial, which was up 16%,  while office leasing dipped 2%, Giamartino said.
This dip, which contrasts with a broader office recovery occurring in the market, is the result of some big deals that slipped into Q4, “which is in part why we have confidence that we’ll see double-digit growth in leasing in Q4.,” she said.
Despite the cautious economic outlook, Sulentic believes that even if things slow down in the U.S. — either because of the interest rate or political environment — CBRE believes growth will accelerate globally, especially in the data center sector.
“Onnec puts us in a great position to take care of that,” Sulentic said. Even if data center growth slows in the U.S., there should be plenty of business involving existing facilities. “We think that in data centers, you’re going to see potentially some pressure on the amount of new build,” he said. “And then what’s happening, and we’re already seeing it, is a lot of refit of existing data centers.”
Outside of its critical infrastructure business, CBRE’s infrastructure services work consists of overseeing the construction of transportation and energy assets along with data centers within project management, as well as sales, leasing and financing for data centers and advisory services. When taking this work into account, CBRE expects its total infrastructure services revenue to spike 40% from this year to $7 billion in 2027, Sulentic said.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft’s Mustafa Suleyman says its AI outperforms doctors on hard cases as he chases ‘medical superintelligence’
articles.title_zh: Microsoft’s Mustafa Suleyman says its AI outperforms doctors on hard cases as he chases ‘medical superintelligence’
articles.content_orig:
Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.
Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.
Microsoft’s AI diagnostic system correctly diagnosed complex medical cases in a simulation more than twice as often as generalist physicians, according to a study published Thursday in Science. Mustafa Suleyman, Microsoft AI’s CEO, called the result a step toward “medical superintelligence.”
The system, dubbed MAI-DxO (DxO for short), coordinates several AI agents that act like a panel of doctors. They question a patient, order tests, and debate a diagnosis.
In a simulation using complex cases from the New England Journal of Medicine, it was correct 83% of the time. Primary care doctors and general internists, working individually with reference materials, were correct 36% of the time. One note: Cases this complex are usually handled by specialists or physician teams, who weren’t part of the comparison.
“There is something very substantial and exciting here,” Dominic King, vice president of Health at Microsoft AI, told TechCrunch. “The biggest challenge in healthcare delivery at the moment is the growing mismatch between demand and supply of medical expertise.”
In publishing these results , Microsoft joins Go o gle and OpenAI in claiming that its AI can match or outperform doctors.
The study’s own data suggests that much of the improvement comes from more powerful underlying AI models, with Microsoft’s orchestration system adding gains on top.
Microsoft tested MAI-DxO with models from several companies, including OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta, and DeepSeek, but its best results came with OpenAI’s GPT-5 and GPT-5.5.
Microsoft measured DxO on cost as well as accuracy, meaning the estimated cost of running the AI on each case. On its own with a short, basic prompt, GPT-5 scored 78.9% on complex cases at about $8,400 per case. DxO cut that cost by about $3,000 but raised accuracy by only about four points. On emergency department cases, there was little improvement in either accuracy or cost improvement between GPT-5 on its own and with the assist from DxO.
With GPT-5.5, a newer model released in April 2026, the results split. On complex cases, DxO increased GPT-5.5’s accuracy score from 72% to nearly 87% at a slightly cheaper cost. However, the gains once again didn’t show up on emergency department cases. Both (with and without DxO) scored about 85% at a similar cost.
DxO helps most on complex cases and with less capable AI models. Gemini 2.5 Flash, for example, scored 46.4% on its own but nearly 69% with DxO. Even so, the gap between the weaker and stronger models was larger than the boost DxO provided.
Microsoft’s researchers said that accuracy gains naturally shrink as models approach the theoretical maximum. “The DxO orchestration helps with the broader challenge of optimization both accuracy and cost,” a spokesperson added.
Suleyman, who leads Microsoft’s effort to build its own frontier AI, told TechCrunch that the company is working with the Mayo Clinic to train a foundation model for healthcare, with release planned for next year. He believes this model will enable the company to “make really enormous leaps here,” and says DxO is part of the foundational infrastructure Microsoft is building to see real breakthroughs in healthcare.
“I really believe that in 2027, we will be on the verge of a coding style breakthrough for medical records,” Suleyman said. “I think we’re going to be able to stream highly accurate predictions about how a medical record might unfold, and obviously that kind of foresight for a clinician is gold dust.”
Suleyman has spent his career trying to use AI to solve medical issues. He was previously a co-founder of DeepMind, which was acquired by Google in 2014. The following year, Google DeepMind acquired King’s startup Hark, a clinical task management app, and the two of them launched DeepMind Health together. Suleyman joined Microsoft to lead its AI unit in 2024, and King followed a few months later.
“We’re just true believers,” Suleyman said.
He said while the use of generative AI in healthcare is still early, he expects healthcare models to get “an order of magnitude better in capability within the next 24 to 36 months.”
“As we’ve seen multiple times in the last five or six years, the progress happens very quickly once you have a flywheel,” Suleyman said. “A flywheel means we have a model in production which we are iterating with real-world usage in order to identify gaps in the model and then patch them and improve them. That’s what’s happened in coding. It’s what happened in chat before that. And I think next year it’s going to start to happen for medical records and for clinical decision support.”
Through a new partnership with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, Microsoft will evaluate the clinical reasoning capabilities of DxO across different hospital settings.
“This technology is ready for real-world evaluations, and you can imagine the complexity and diversity of issues that come from a Boston emergency department on a Friday evening,” King said.
He explained how the study will work: Patients will get standard treatment, including triage, time with a specialist, treatments, investigations, and decision on whether it’s safe to discharge. In parallel, those who consent will also engage with DxO. Microsoft and its partners will compare DxO’s recommendations against the human doctors’.
Google published a clinical study alongside Beth Israel in The Lancet this month to evaluate Google’s AMIE conversational diagnostic AI in real-world urgent care visits, while human physicians monitored the interactions in real time.
“We think this will be the biggest study of its kind,” King said. “It will be across not just emergency settings but urgent care environments, and will give us very compelling evidence by the end of the study period around the ability for these systems to be deployed at greater scale in the future.”
Microsoft’s study in Science coincides with a manifesto of sorts around what it will take to build medical superintelligence, defined as “the capacity to surpass the strongest contemporary human-led health systems in medical reasoning and coordination across the full arc of care.” Microsoft hopes to move beyond benchmarking individual tasks — like answering medical exam questions and generating diagnoses — into integrating with clinicians and healthcare systems for better outcomes.
“This is the kind of technology that everybody in the world wants, and that’s why we’re committed to doing everything we can to accelerate its introduction to the world,” Suleyman said, adding that this focus could be a differentiator for Microsoft compared to the other frontier labs.
Microsoft already sells dictation and radiology tools to clinicians and sees DxO as an expansion to those efforts.
“We have to have the absolute number one state-of-the-art medical clinical decision support products over the next few years,” Suleyman said.

articles.title_orig: Final Israeli polls point to stalemate ahead of Tuesday’s election
articles.title_zh: Final Israeli polls point to stalemate ahead of Tuesday’s election
articles.content_orig:
With no more polls allowed to be released before the election, neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition is reaching the 61-seats necessary for an outright majority
ack GUEZ / AFP via Getty Images
A road sign stands in front of a large billboard featuring Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu (R) of the Likud party and former military chief and leader of the centrist Yashar party, Gadi Eisenkot, in Ramat Gan on October 20, 2026.
The likeliest outcome of Israel’s upcoming election is a stalemate , according to the final polls ahead of next Tuesday’s election, with neither side — Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc and the bloc opposing him, led by Gadi Eisenkot — projected to reach a majority of the Knesset.
Israeli law prohibits the publication of new polls from Friday until the Oct. 27 election.
The overall polling average put the bloc led by Netanyahu ahead, with 54 seats, while the opposition would get 50 seats, both short of the necessary 61-seat majority. Netanyahu’s Likud polled at 23 seats compared to 21 for Eisenkot’s Yashar party.
However, the gap between polls from right-leaning news outlets and those from the mainstream networks and publications was significant.
In the average of six mainstream TV and newspaper polls, the Eisenkot-led bloc had more seats than the current coalition. An average of polls from the last two days showed Eisenkot’s bloc narrowly ahead, holding 52 seats to the Netanyahu bloc’s 50 seats.
Meanwhile, an average of the polls on Israel’s Channel 14 and i24 News, which use pollsters who had previously worked for Likud, found Netanyahu’s coalition projected to receive a 61-seat majority of the Knesset, while Eisenkot’s bloc would only have 45 seats.
The Arab parties, the Joint List and Ra’am, are polling at an average of 14 seats, just short of their record 15 seats in 2020 when they ran together.
Arab voter turnout has hovered around the 50% mark in the last decade. However, Stat-Net, a polling institute specializing in the Israeli Arab population, has said that it may be as high as 68-69% this year, which may give the parties representing the Arab minority even more seats than projected.
Increased Arab turnout would contribute to higher overall turnout, which would increase the number of votes needed to meet the minimal threshold to enter the Knesset.
In both the general polling average and the right-leaning media’s polls, neither Amcha Yisrael nor the Reservists and Economy Party, which have hovered near the 3.25% electoral threshold in recent weeks, received enough votes to enter the Knesset. In the more left-leaning polls, Reservists and Economy, which has not pledged to recommend either Netanyahu or Eisenkot for prime minister, receives an average of three seats.

Blu-ray is fading after 20 years in the market, with Sony Japan finally discontinuing its last dedicated Blu-ray player. According to FlatpanelsHD , Sony Japan has finally marked the UBP-X700/K player as “Discontinued,” meaning customers in the country can no longer purchase a new standalone Blu-ray player from the company. This should not come as a surprise, as Sony stopped shipping the players in February of this year, suggesting that Sony only relied on existing inventory for its remaining Blu-ray player sales.
The PlayStation 5 is the only remaining Sony device that can play Blu-ray discs, but the company has also announced that it will end physical game disc production by January 2028. Because of this, some people fear that the upcoming PlayStation 6 will no longer have an optical drive. This move follows in the footsteps of LG , which ended Blu-ray player production in 2024. Japanese electronics companies Elecom and Buffalo have also ended production of Blu-ray drives for PCs this year, although Buffalo Americas says that it is “fully committed to supplying optical drives to the American market, and our DVD/Blu-ray drive products are anticipated to remain available for the near future.”
This move away from physical media and focus on streaming is worrying, especially to those who are concerned that we are moving towards a world where people no longer own anything. Because of this, sales of “retro media,” including CDs and vinyl, went up by 59% and 18% respectively . While you could still purchase a Blu-ray player from other manufacturers like Panasonic, Sony is one of the bigger companies that built and supported the standard, and its move to end the production and sale of Blu-ray players will leave this niche market even smaller. The audiophile market is facing the same dilemma, as some Hi-Fi player manufacturers ended production of selected products because optical drive makers have stopped making the components needed to read SACDs .
Ultra HD Blu-ray is facing the same upheaval that VHS and DVDs went through with the introduction of new formats. But while the older technologies were replaced by higher-quality formats, Blu-ray is being replaced not by more pixels, but by the convenience of streaming. However, it also comes with the caveat that people would no longer own physical media; a trend that worries data archivists.

articles.title_orig: TV Reporter, Bystander Save Man From Sinking Car
articles.title_zh: TV Reporter, Bystander Save Man From Sinking Car
articles.content_orig:
A driver has been rescued by two bystanders, including an ABC reporter, from his sinking car in floodwater north of Brisbane.
The man drove his four-wheel-drive at speed through water on Buchanan Road at Morayfield.
The car stalled and started to sink.
ABC reporter Will Murray swimming to the sinking car. ( ABC News )
ABC reporter Will Murray and Daniel Hainey swam out to the car and pulled the driver out of the vehicle.
About 170 millimetres of rain has fallen in the area since this morning.
Speaking after a shower and some lunch, Murray said he was relieved everyone was OK.
"I saw him drive in and immediately his car started floating downstream so I rang Triple Zero," he said.
"On the phone the operator asked me if I could see the driver and if I thought he could get free.
"Initially I could see him, but he disappeared from my sight within seconds so I made the call to jump in."
Murray said he handed the phone to his colleague, camera operator Liz Pickering, and started swimming towards the sinking car.
The two rescuers pulled the man from the car just before it went under water. ( ABC News )
"When we got to the car we tried to open the closest door, no luck, then got on the back of the car with the thought to break the back window," he said.
"I thought to try the passenger side rear door first and put my feet against the car and pulled as hard as I could and with some luck the door swung open.
"I think water rushing in helped create some pressure to force the door open."
Murray said the driver was then able to make his way to the open door, and the rescuers pulled him to safety and shallow waters.
"All three of us gave each other a big hug and were just so relieved," he said.
"It was very scary, but happy everyone is safe and relieved it is OK.
"I just witnessed how quickly it can go south and it is terrifying. Please don't drive into floodwaters."
Mr Hainey, who rescued the man alongside Murray, said he was out with his family when he saw the ute but did not realise someone was inside until the window moved.
"The car began to slowly sink deeper and deeper, and that's when I thought, 'Oh no, this is not looking good', so I started swimming in there," he said.
Mr Hainey said the driver was "very, very lucky".
The Queensland Fire Department advises all residents not to swim in floodwater.
Pickering was on scene filming overlay footage of the flooded road when the incident occurred.
She captured the incident on video as the men rescued the driver from the vehicle.
ABC reporter Will Murray and another man pull a man from a sinking car. ( ABC News )
Murray said emergency services arrived about 10 minutes after the rescue.
"We were chatting with the man and he was saying he didn't see the signage and didn't realise how deep it was," Murray said.
"I had no idea how deep it was and that's the lesson we keep hearing, isn't it, that you can't tell and you really couldn't; it didn't look particularly severe.
"But as you can see in the vision, the car completely disappears, it's clearly very deep in the middle there."
Speaking about being called a hero or a lifesaver, Murray quickly diverted attention to the men and women who work for emergency services.
He said he has a greater respect for the work they do.
"The adrenaline is still very, very high. I don't know how people do this regularly," he said.

WASHINGTON, D.C.—Consumer Reports (CR) today called for Millie Moon to recall its diapers , based on the growing number and severity of incidents reported to the Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC). CR is advising parents and caregivers to stop using Millie Moon diapers while the cause of the infant skin reactions is investigated.
Gabe Knight, senior safety policy advocate for Consumer Reports, said, “When reports pour in of babies suffering painful rashes, and hundreds of them mention the same diaper brand, that’s a serious problem that should prompt immediate action from the company and the government. Millie Moon should issue a recall together with the CPSC to prevent additional infants from being harmed.
“While we understand the company’s investigation is ongoing, there are simply too many reported incidents and injuries to wait any longer. Diaper rash might be a common malady, but it’s highly unusual for this many reports to be tied to one brand in such a short period. It’s time for Millie Moon to take action to keep infants safe and provide meaningful remedies to families whose babies have suffered harm,” Knight added.
More than 600 incidents involving Millie Moon diapers have been submitted to the CPSC this year, according to Consumer Reports’ review of the agency’s public database, SaferProducts.gov . Parents describe rashes, redness, bleeding, swelling, blisters, peeling, and other skin reactions. Numerous reports describe medical treatment, including at least three emergency-room visits. In CR’s review, no other brand of diapers comes close to this level of incidents during the same period.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft says its AI tool is better than doctors at diagnosing conditions
articles.title_zh: Microsoft says its AI tool is better than doctors at diagnosing conditions
articles.content_orig:
‘We’re going to build something that is indistinguishable from human performance … in the next couple of years,’ Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman tells The Verge.
‘We’re going to build something that is indistinguishable from human performance … in the next couple of years,’ Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman tells The Verge.
For years, AI leaders have touted healthcare as one of the clearest examples of where their technology will improve lives. Now “it is finally here,” Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman tells The Verge . The company claims to have developed an AI-powered tool it says can diagnose conditions up to four times more accurately than human doctors.
The findings, published Thursday in one of the world’s most prestigious journals, Science , are based on tests pitting Microsoft’s AI system against human physicians on a series of scenarios drawn from medical case reports and emergency department data. Microsoft compiled the cases into its own benchmark, SDBench, which it plans to open-source. Designed to function like a panel of medical experts, Microsoft’s Diagnostic Orchestrator uses multiple AI agents to reason through symptoms and medical histories, decide what tests to order, and arrive at a diagnosis, mimicking the process doctors use to investigate cases.
On cases taken from hundreds of reports published in The New England Journal of Medicine , Microsoft’s system achieved a diagnostic accuracy of around 83 percent, compared with roughly 36 percent for generalist physicians using references and 22 percent for those working without them. The Diagnostic Orchestrator also outperformed doctors on emergency department cases drawn from a large database of patient admissions at the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, scoring 80 percent accuracy compared with an average of 47 percent for human physicians. The AI system also tended to reach its diagnoses at a lower estimated cost than human counterparts.
The researchers say that the system, which is powered by OpenAI’s GPT-5, also outperformed frontier AI models operating on their own, though the peer-reviewed paper does not include newer models like GPT-6 Astra , Meta’s Muse Wonder Full , Google’s Gemini 4 Argon , or Anthropic’s Opus 5.5 . The Diagnostic Orchestrator was first developed when GPT-4.1 was the most advanced model available, but the researchers say subsequent testing suggests that “improvements in model capability do not necessarily diminish the benefits” of having multiple agents work together.
Microsoft acknowledges there’s a long road ahead before the technology can be widely deployed. While the tests more closely mirror the way doctors diagnose conditions — asking questions, weighing possible explanations, and ordering tests before reaching a diagnosis — the system has only been tested on past medical cases and it remains unclear how well it would perform in real clinical settings. “It needs clinical validation,” Suleyman says. “That is a leap, but this is a major milestone along that journey.”
The research is part of a broader ambition at Microsoft to develop what the company calls “medical superintelligence” — AI that can outperform the best human-led healthcare systems. Microsoft has used the term “superintelligence” since before Donald Trump and his administration co-opted it as a catch-all replacement for “AI.”
Diagnosis is just part of Microsoft’s health vision, says the company’s AI health lead, Dr. Dominic King, a coauthor of the study. In a blog post published Thursday and a forthcoming article in the BMJ Digital Health & AI medical journal, the company outlines five other areas it believes AI will need to master, including coordinating clinical care, making treatment decisions, and handling the human side of medicine.
King tells The Verge that Microsoft plans to begin testing the system in hospital settings with the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center to see how it performs in real-world clinical environments. Neither King nor Suleyman would commit to a firm timeline, though King says it will likely “get underway in the next couple of months.”
Commercialization could also be on the horizon, though Microsoft has yet to say when or how the technology might become available. The company already has a significant presence in US healthcare through its digital tools, and health is one of the most popular uses for its consumer-facing chatbot Copilot . King emphasizes the need for a responsible rollout, noting the high regulatory and compliance requirements in medicine that would need to be followed.
“Next year we’re going to see extremely impressive deployments of intelligent systems in production,” Suleyman says. “I think that this is just going to change the way care is delivered in a big way.”
Suleyman has spoken previously about his “human-centered” vision for AI, and said medicine is no exception. Even as he predicts the arrival of “something that is indistinguishable from human performance on medical superintelligence in the next couple of years,” he insists that human clinicians should and will always have a central role in patient care.
While he acknowledges AI could end up with doctors being handed more work, he says his hope is that it will take some of “the drudgery” out of medicine, freeing up clinicians to spend more time with patients.
“I’m very optimistic about what’s coming next,” he says. “I think this is why we build technology.”

articles.title_orig: Nintendo Switch 2 Gets Its First Software-Only Jailbreak, With Help From OpenAI Codex
articles.title_zh: Nintendo Switch 2 Gets Its First Software-Only Jailbreak, With Help From OpenAI Codex
articles.content_orig:
A security researcher has demonstrated a software-only partial jailbreak of the Switch 2, gaining “userland” access that he says “lets us run homebrew, reverse engineer and mod Switch 2 games, back up save files off the Switch, and access most of the Switch 2’s peripherals through MMIO.”
The hack relies on the original Switch version of SmileBasic 4 , the latest in a long-running series of programming environments and interpreters that run on Nintendo hardware. The so-called “tethered” hack also requires access to a macOS or Linux PC on the same network to run a node.js package that helps enable privileged system access.
Researcher Sammy Hajhamid writes that he used OpenAI’s Codex to poke at SmileBasic’s language interpreter, using a custom harness that could send USB commands to the system and view results via HDMI (as well as power cycling via a Bluetooth light switch flipping device). After “substantial effort for ~2 weeks,” that harness discovered a 32-bit integer overflow that occurs when removing items from an array in SmileBasic. That error gives access to an array pointer, which in turn allows read and write access to portions of system memory.
From there, Hajhamid writes that he started poking around for access to the Switch 2’s internal sysmodules, looking for ones that could provide more privileged access to the console’s core functions. Eventually, he found a buffer overflow in the console’s FileSystem services module that exposed a cached data pointer, granting arbitrary read and write privileges. From there, Hajhamid writes that he could execute “privileged filesystem actions” and eventually achieve native code execution through a faked filesystem process.
Hajhamid, who goes by Pepsipu online, showed off a host of new modded characters in Mario Kart World as a proof of concept for the exploit. Others are similarly showing off simple demos and in-progress developer tools running on exploited hardware.
Full Vulkan GPU working in userland by u/Icy-ConcentrationC in switch2hacks
Still, the current “userland” exploit keeps any Switch 2 homebrew developers trapped in a relatively small sandbox, and falls well short of the kernel-level access that would provide full control of the hardware.
If the SmileBasic name sounds familiar to you, it’s probably because the 3DS version of the same software was key to the so-called smilehax exploit on that handheld back in 2016. Nintendo removed SmileBasic from the 3DS eShop shortly after that hack became public, and SmileBasic 4 has similarly already been delisted from the Switch eShop worldwide (though a Japanese demo version that may work similarly is still accessible as of this story’s publication).
That delisting could help slow the spread of this exploit to the wider base of Switch 2 owners that haven’t previously purchased and/or downloaded SmileBasic. But others in the Switch 2 hacking community are already teasing some similar exploits that appear to work using other games. And while the current exploit works on the latest Switch 2 firmware version (23.0.1), this particular vulnerability seems likely to be patched out in imminent firmware releases, which will be required for continued access to many Nintendo services and future game releases.
So while this exploit is definitely unwelcome news for Nintendo, it’s not nearly as problematic as the “unpatchable” original Switch exploit that surfaced in 2018 . That hack required a complete hardware redesign to ensure that future systems were not susceptible.
Still, the fact that Switch 2 hackers have gotten this far just over a year after the console’s release is not a good sign for the overall impregnability of Nintendo’s system software. Get ready for another never-ending cycle between console hackers and the hardware makers trying to keep them out of their console’s deepest recesses.

Oracle's cloud backlog is surging past $664 billion while free cash flow sits deep in negative territory, and the CFO refused to name a date when that flips. Something has to give, and figuring out which side breaks first changes…
Oracle ( NYSE:ORCL | ORCL Price Prediction ) trades at $131.14. Its low multiple used to look like a bargain, but now it looks like a fair price for a company that has to borrow and issue stock to build its AI cloud.
Oracle sells databases, enterprise applications and, more and more, AI training and inference capacity. Cloud now makes up 60% of total revenue, up from 48% a year ago. The stock has fallen 52.08% over the past year and sits far below its 52-week high of $283.40.
Bulls point to the price. At about 16x the $8.10 non-GAAP EPS guide for this fiscal year, and roughly 12x the $10.9916 consensus for next year, Oracle costs less than many slower-growing software names. Its PEG ratio is 0.807.
The growth is real. Cloud infrastructure revenue rose 121% to $7.39 billion, and remaining performance obligations reached $664 billion. GPU use was 97.9%, and renewed capacity was repriced at a 20% premium to prior contracts. Analysts made 35 upward and 1 downward full-year EPS revisions over the past 30 days.
Free cash flow was negative $5.4 billion last quarter, following negative $23.7 billion in fiscal 2026. Management still expects $90 billion to $95 billion in capex this year. Interest expense rose 55% to $1.4 billion. After completing a $20 billion equity sale, Oracle plans to raise about $40 billion more through debt and equity.
The chief financial officer declined to say when free cash flow turns positive: “We haven’t given a particular timeframe on that yet.” Gross margins are also expected to step down. A CNBC Fast Money panelist put it bluntly: “There are plenty of other ways to play this story with better balance sheets.”
Management expects around half of RPO to convert into sales over the next 36 months. Next quarter’s guide calls for revenue growth of 30% to 34% and EPS of $1.85 to $1.93. If Oracle hits those numbers and gives a free cash flow timeline, today’s price could prove too low. If margins slip or financing costs keep rose, it could still fall further.
The average analyst target is $237.36, meaning about 81% upside. That figure comes from 43 analysts. Price targets are one data point, and none of them are guarantees:
Oracle is down 31.85% year to date, while the S&P 500 is up 12.78%. Over the past month, Oracle fell 10.88% as the index gained 0.97%. Shares trade below both the 50-day ($144.77) and 200-day ($159.87) moving averages.
At $131.14, Oracle’s risks outweigh its cheap multiple.
Oracle beat on growth and the stock still fell, which tells you investors now care more about funding than about bookings. Shares gave up an early post-earnings gain and ended the day down nearly 2% even after Oracle beat estimates. Downside could come within the next two quarters from more dilution, rising interest costs and lower near-term estimates. Analysts already made 23 downward revisions to the February-quarter EPS estimate in 30 days.
A firm free cash flow timeline, or proof that operating margins are expanding as capacity increases, would change this view. Until one of those shows up, the low multiple reflects real balance sheet risk.
A low multiple only pays off if the cash eventually reaches shareholders, and Oracle has yet to show when that happens.

articles.title_zh: Brazilian election: Lula seeks Bolsonaro's disqualification over alleged Meta interference
articles.content_orig:
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's campaign has requested the disqualification of right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in the lead up to the final round of the presidential election on Sunday over alleged interference by social media company Meta.
In a petition filed to the country's top electoral court on Wednesday, the leftist incumbent president accused Meta, the tech giant behind Whatsapp, Instagram and Facebook, of limiting its content to boost Bolsonaro's campaign.
In response, Bolsonaro filed a petition seeking to disqualify Lula over what he said was the mass dissemination of government posts on WhatsApp.
The company has denied the campaigns have been treated unequally.
It comes after UN experts said on Wednesday that they were concerned about reports of discrepancies in the ability of each campaign to reach voters on Meta's platforms.
A report led by the UN's special rapporteur on freedom of expression said Meta must ensure a level playing field online during the election.
It cited incidents including "temporary interruptions of one candidate's campaign account; differences in audience engagement, user feeds, view counts and reach; restrictions on that campaign's Instagram posts".
"Information, including from Meta employees, suggests that accounts linked to one side of the presidential race were disproportionately curtailed," it read.
Meta has denied taking action to favour one side of the election and has said it would comply with an order from a Brazilian court to treat Bolsonaro and Lula equally.
Lula's campaign had previously filed a complaint alleging that accounts and content related to Bolsonaro were boosted.
Users also reported that Meta's artificial intelligence tools were not generating images related to Lula.
Brazilians will head to the polls on Sunday as Lula seeks a fourth term in office.
Bolsonaro beat Lula in the first round of voting on 4 October by a narrow margin, but fell short of the 50% of valid votes needed to win outright.
On Wednesday, Lula's campaign filed a petition to Brazil's Superior Electoral Court (TSE) for Bolsonaro and Alfredo Gaspar, his candidate for vice-president, to be investigated over "abuse of economic power and improper use of social network".
The petition also seeks to make Bolsonaro ineligible to stand for election for eight years following the 2026 election.
Meanwhile, Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former president Jair Bolsonaro, accused his rival of "abuse of political and economic power".
He claims the government has used personal data taken from official databases to send mass messages on Whatsapp to promote social programmes.
Opinion polls suggest Sunday's run-off will be extremely close, with little separating the two as Brazil's 159 million registered voters prepare to go to the ballot boxes.

American Express is bringing Airbnb into its travel rewards platform.
The companies on Thursday announced a new partnership to bring more than 1 million Airbnb listings to Amex's travel portal and allow cardholders to earn rewards when booking the stays. It does not currently allow members to redeem points to pay for Airbnb bookings.
The launch adds Airbnb rentals to Amex's hotel portfolio, which includes more than 3,400 properties across its Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection programs.

"We're excited to bring more choice and flexibility to American Express Card Members with this exclusive partnership. Both of our companies exist to help people travel more and better, and this partnership helps people see more of the world by making travel more rewarding," said Juan David Borrero, head of partnerships at Airbnb, in a news release.

The changes come as competition among premium credit cards continues to ramp up.
Last year, American Express raised the annual fee on its premium Platinum card to $895. In turn, it's been investing in cardholder perks such as new lounges in airports and at big-ticket events and experiences as a way to attract more high-paying customers.
Earlier this month, it announced an expansion of its Centurion Lounges , with renovations coming to four existing lounges and new ones planned for Newark Liberty International Airport and London Heathrow Airport. The Newark lounge will be the largest in its network.
The partnership also comes as Americans continue to opt for travel and luxury experiences, even as prices for airfare, gas and hotels rise. articles.title_orig: Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield, and what they mean to Ukraine in the war against Russia
articles.title_zh: Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield, and what they mean to Ukraine in the war against Russia
articles.content_orig:
Over the past week, Ukraine has received a stark reminder of its growing dependence on uninterrupted access to Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield networks in its drone-heavy war against Russia, now in its fifth year.
Ukraine has a fraction of Russia's resources, but its aggressive development of drone warfare on defensive and offensive fronts has helped it endure an onslaught from its much bigger adversary, which invaded Ukraine in early 2022. That was true until last week, when Ukraine reported a throttling of the Starshield network that was causing its drones to stop midflight and fall out of the sky.
The two SpaceX networks operate on a constellation of thousands of low-Earth satellites — Starlink is the commercial version, while Starshield is a military product licensed to the U.S. government and its partners, among them Ukraine.
Kyiv's reliance on drones has made Starlink and Starshield nearly indispensable to its arsenal. When Ukraine experienced a disruption to those networks, it lost the shield of interceptors and drones that offered some protection against Russian drone and missile strikes.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy believes Musk throttled Starshield at the request of U.S. officials , though the world's richest man has denied any role and said it's the U.S. government that controls the military-grade network. President Trump has also denied he's responsible for slowing the network.
However, CBS News reported Tuesday that Musk was behind the disruption, which occurred after he spoke with administration officials multiple times seeking clarity on the president's thinking on the matter, according to sources familiar with the situation.
There has also been conflicting information about whether full access to the networks has been restored. As of Wednesday afternoon, Starlink remained throttled, Zelenskyy's office confirmed.
Here's what's known about Starshield and Starlink — and their role in the Ukraine war.
On Oct. 13, Ukraine's military began experiencing sudden difficulties with Starshield equipment, making it more difficult to carry out missions with fast-moving drones, officials and soldiers told CBS News .
Ukrainian soldiers said they noticed "speed limits" had been imposed on their use of SpaceX's Starshield internet dishes, the military-grade Starlink dishes that Ukrainians strap onto their drones so remote pilots can maintain their connection with the unmanned aircraft as they fly toward Russian targets.
Access was restricted by turning off dishes on Ukrainian drones flying above a certain speed, causing them to fall out of the sky. Ukraine's Ministry of Defense sources said SpaceX had unilaterally imposed the Starshield restrictions without informing them beforehand.
Zelenskyy said Saturday the speed limits had prevented Ukraine from using Starshield to shoot down Russian Shahed attack drones.
Starshield, the military-grade satellite network, runs on the same constellation of satellites as its civilian sister, Starlink, but has fewer technical limitations and more advanced security features. Both are operated by Musk's company SpaceX.
The U.S. government pays SpaceX to license the use of Starshield and controls who can access the technology. Its use has been limited to Ukraine and occupied territories. It is not available in Russia.
There is no working alternative to Starlink, as no direct competitor approaches Starlink's coverage of 11,150 satellites. Amazon Leo aims to compete, but at this point, it has under 400 satellites in low Earth orbit and has been hampered by the launchpad explosion of a Blue Origin rocket in May.
Regular Starlink terminals have a 70 km/hr (43.5 mph) speed cap, which is the speed at which internet can be used in a vehicle in motion. At rates exceeding the cap, the internet degrades and is no longer usable.
Starshield has no artificial speed cap and is known to work at speeds of at least 160 km/hr (99.4 mph). Starshield-equipped strike drones cruise at 160 km/h or more, and they're the backbone of Ukrainian mid-range strikes.
During the throttling over the last week, Ukrainian units reported link drops at speeds as low as 90 km/hr (55.9 mph), making those drones inoperable. The degradation of Starshield is estimated to have cost Ukraine tens of millions of dollars in losses, according to an analysis by Dimko Zhluktenko, a drone pilot and analyst in the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
On Oct. 15, some Ukrainian officials said that the Starshield restrictions had been lifted. But Zelenskyy told NBC News on Sunday the maximum speed was still 161 km/hr.
Zelenskyy told Fox News on Wednesday that the service was "still limited," but he added that Secretary of State Marco Rubio told him he would "work with his team on this to unblock" it.
It uses both. Starlink has been providing internet service to Ukrainian civilians and military forces since 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, according to Reuters .
Initially funded by private donors and a U.S. foreign aid contract, SpaceX won a Pentagon contract to pay for Starlink for Ukraine in 2023, along with a contract for 500 Starshield terminals.
In August 2024, SpaceX signed another Defense Department contract to expand Starshield usage to 3,000 terminals for the front lines, Bloomberg reported.

articles.title_orig: US weekly jobless claims near 57-year lows, underscore labor market stability
articles.title_zh: US weekly jobless claims near 57-year lows, underscore labor market stability
articles.content_orig:
Employers continue to hold onto workers even as hiring remains weak, sending weekly jobless claims to around their lowest levels in records that stretch back nearly six decades.
Initial filings for unemployment insurance slipped to a seasonally adjusted 194,000 for the week ended Oct. 17, the Labor Department reported Thursday.
That marked another leg lower in the low-fire trend, with the total just off the 189,000 reported for the week of July 18 that was the lowest since September 1969. Claims have averaged 212,000 over the past year, and the four-week moving average is down to 197,750.
Those numbers come against an uncertain backdrop for the labor market.
Nonfarm payrolls rose by just 29,000 in September and have averaged a gain of just 69,000 a month in 2026. The unemployment rate rose to 4.2%, an increase largely due to a sharp spike in labor force participation. Layoffs have remained modest, declining by 61,000 in August, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data released Sept. 29.
Over the prior 12 months, the layoff rate measured as a share of the total workforce fell to 1%, down 0.2 percentage point during the period. Job openings were relatively flat during the period.
"Despite extremely pessimistic views expressed in consumer confidence surveys regarding the economy overall, countless headlines describing job cuts from a variety of businesses, and the phantom job-stealing power of AI, the claims data suggests that labor market conditions are stable," Thomas Simons, chief U.S. economist at Jefferies, said in a client note.
The data comes during the reference week that the BLS uses to calculate the payrolls growth number. The October jobs report will be released Nov. 6.
Federal Reserve officials gather next week to issue their latest decision on interest rates . Policymakers in recent days have characterized the labor market as a source of general strength and focused more of their attention on the nettlesome inflation problem that has kept the pace of price increases well above the central bank's 2% target.
Markets expect the Fed to hold off on a rate hike in October but then to institute another quarter percentage point increase in December.

articles.title_orig: Who blinked first? Fragile EU-China trade peace sparks new war of words
articles.title_zh: Who blinked first? Fragile EU-China trade peace sparks new war of words
articles.content_orig:
As European officials flag more trade restrictions, Beijing bristles at the idea it can be pushed into yielding to Brussels’ demands
In Brussels and Berlin, officials are emboldened by what they consider proof that collective EU pressure can force Chinese concessions. Rather than resting on their laurels, they are cooking up a fresh batch of trade restrictions.
Beijing, on the other hand, has bristled at the idea that it can be strong-armed into yielding to Europe’s demands, even more so the suggestion that further concessions may be coming. State media has carried numerous warnings against European hubris.
It has resulted in an awkward, terse trade peace: an agreement that was supposed to defuse a trade war has led to both sides, rhetorically at least, hardening their positions. With verbal volleys flying back and forth, doubts are already surfacing over whether this delicate ceasefire can hold until the next round of negotiations in January.

articles.title_orig: Global Rush to Fix Security Flaw Uncovered by A.I. Leaves Sites Offline
articles.title_zh: Global Rush to Fix Security Flaw Uncovered by A.I. Leaves Sites Offline
articles.content_orig:
Government and company websites around the world briefly went dark and suspended some services, as operators scrambled to patch their systems after artificial intelligence helped find critical vulnerabilities in a widely used programming language.
Nearly three dozen UK government services are unavailable and four are “partially unavailable” while security upgrades take place, UK government minister Elizabeth Lloyd told the House of Lords Thursday. “No large public-facing critical services are being affected by the exercise but some limited services may temporarily be offline while security work is carried out,” a UK government spokesperson told reporters.
The US National Security Agenc y and Europe’s cybersecurity agency have advised companies to take immediate action to address two critical flaws in PHP, a programming language that powers 70% of all websites in the world, including WordPress and Drupal, an open-source content management system.
The PHP Foundation, the organization behind the coding language, has released a patch for the bugs, which have been hidden in their software for years, and is urging website operators to update their systems immediately.
Popular Irish news website The Journal was temporarily offline Thursday morning while it bolstered its “defences,” it said in a notice. The Journal is Ireland’s second most-used online news source, behind only RTÉ, the national broadcaster, according to the Reuters Institute.
The flaws in PHP – which originally stood for Personal Home Page – were uncovered by teams at OpenAI , Google-owned cybersecurity company Wiz, and another cybersecurity company, Calif . The bugs, collectively called PHP2Shell, could allow attackers to hack into websites and read memory that could contain sensitive information, like passwords.
“With PHP behind such a vast share of the web, the exposure could reach almost everywhere people spend money online,” said Nigel Green, the CEO of deVere Group, a financial advisory firm.
“Booking platforms, marketplaces, subscription services, ticketing sites, delivery apps and utility portals could all be holding card details on systems built with the same kind of code,” he added.
Even world leaders urged organizations to take action. Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said that his cabinet was “closely monitoring the situation surrounding the vulnerabilities in PHP.”
Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said companies should consider suspending services if necessary in order to reduce their exposure. “Please check if your publicly available websites use PHP, and prepare to apply the fix patch that will be released tonight… as soon as possible,” she posted on X Wednesday.
Japanese airline ANA, railway operator JR West and the country’s largest bank, MUFG, were among companies that reported some webpages and services temporarily suspended.
In Europe, government websites in France, Denmark, Finland and the Netherlands, including the Dutch cyber security agency, were temporarily taken offline while security fixes were implemented.
The Wikimedia Foundation, the non-profit that operates Wikipedia, told CNN Thursday that it was “in the process of addressing security vulnerabilities in PHP,” and that a number of its systems had been taken down as a “precautionary measure.”
AI played a crucial role in finding and fixing vulnerabilities “that had remained hidden in the PHP codebase for more than a decade,” according to Wiz, which said the episode marks an “AI inflection point.”
“What AI changed was the ability to understand the weaknesses and turn them into a working exploit,” Wiz researchers wrote in a blog post Wednesday in which they described PHP as a “backbone of the web.”
“With frontier AI models and the right tools, a single researcher completed in a week what previously would have taken a world-class team months of work,” they added.
The bugs were discovered in late August but were disclosed to the public only on Wednesday, after PHP had come up with a fix.
The flaws could allow attackers to remotely execute code, disrupt services and expose customer data, according to web infrastructure provider Cloudflare, which has been working with the PHP Foundation, Calif, OpenAI and Wiz to address the issue.
Researchers at Wiz used Google’s Gemini 4 Argon, Wiz Atlas and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol during the research process.
Wiz researchers say the issue is on par with the Heartbleed bug from 2014, which impacted an encryption technology estimated to be used by two-thirds of the Web. Heartbleed allowed cybercriminals to access data that should have been protected.
Like Heartbleed, the researchers at Wiz say PHP2Shell could similarly serve as a turning point in cybersecurity. While the vulnerabilities existed for years, AI made it practical to deploy them.
“The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve,” the researchers said.
“Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”
– CNN’s John Liu, Anna Cooban, Amy Croffey and James Frater contributed reporting.
